<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
Let $m\ge1$, $r\ge0$, $s=\min\{m,r\}$, and
\[
\mu_j=\binom{m+r-1}{s-j}-\binom{m+r-1}{s-j-1}.
\]
With the conventions $\binom n{-1}=0$ and
$\binom{[n]}{-1}=\varnothing$, for every commutative ring $R$,
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};R)\cong\ker U_{r-1}(m+r-1).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})
 \cong\bigoplus_{j=2}^{s}(\mathbb{Z}/j)^{\mu_j}.
\]
In particular this torsion group is zero for $r=0,1$.
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:intro-orderk}
Let $k\ge2$, and let $q(k)$ be the largest prime power dividing $k$.
For $m\ge1$ and $r\ge0$, the group
\[
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})
\]
contains a direct summand $\mathbb{Z}/k$ if and only if
\[
m\ge q(k),\qquad r\ge q(k).
\]
In particular, every finite order occurs in the integral homology of a graph
braid group: for $q=q(k)$, the group
\[
H_{q-1}(\mathbb{B}_qK_{q+1,2q-1};\mathbb{Z})
\]
contains a direct summand $\mathbb{Z}/k$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item For $q\ge2$ and $m\ge q$, there are explicit matching-indexed chains
$w_m,z_m$ on $K_{m+1,m+q-1}$ with
\[
\partial w_m=qz_m,\qquad \partial z_m=0,\qquad \operatorname{ord}[z_m]=q.
\]
For prime $q=p$, $[z_m]$ generates the entire $p$-primary part.
\item Let $m\ge2$, $r\ge1$, and write $A,B$ for the parts of sizes $m+1,m+r-1$.
The generalized theta classes $x_{B'}$ supported on
$K_{A,B'}$, $B'\in\binom B{m-1}$, generate a subgroup, and
$\delta_T\mapsto x_{B\setminus T}$, $T\in\binom Br$, induces an isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(m+r-1)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }
\langle x_{B'}\rangle\subseteq H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z}).
\]
All relations are generated by
$\sum_{B'\subset C,\ |B'|=m-1}x_{B'}=0$ for $C\in\binom Bm$,
and this subgroup contains the entire torsion subgroup.
Every $x_{B'}$ has infinite order for $1\le r\le m-1$.
For $r\ge m$, the subgroup is exactly the torsion subgroup, and
every $x_{B'}$ has order $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,m)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- theoremc-1: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item Let $q=p^a$ with $p$ prime and $a\ge1$, let $m\ge q$, and put $K=K_{m+1,m+q-1}$.
      The $p$-primary part of $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$ has exactly one cyclic summand of order
      $q$, and all its other summands have smaller order.  For every $\Gamma<K$, the
      group $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ has no element of order $q$.
\item $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5};\mathbb{Z})$ has odd torsion, whereas $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ has no odd torsion
      for every $\Gamma<K_{4,5}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremc-1 -->
<!-- theoremd-1: body_md -->
For $m\ge1$ and $a,b\ge m$, there is a multiplicity-free decomposition
\[
 H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Q})\cong
 \bigoplus_{\substack{\lambda\vdash m\\
 \lambda_1\le a-m,\ \lambda'_1\le b-m}}
 S^{(a-m,\lambda)}\boxtimes S^{(b-m,\lambda')}.
\]
If $m\ge2$, $a,b\ge2m-1$, and $p\ge m$ is an odd prime, then
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})$ has no $p$-primary torsion.
<!-- end theoremd-1 -->
<!-- theoreme-1: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item Let $q\ge2$, $m\ge q$, and $r\ge q$. The inclusion
      \[
      K_{m+1,m+q-1}\hookrightarrow K_{m+1,m+r-1}
      \]
      sends the explicit class $[z_m^{(q)}]$ of Theorem~B to an element
      of order exactly $q$. When $m=q=p$ is prime, it induces an
      isomorphism on $p$-primary torsion, with both groups equal to $\mathbb{Z}/p$.
\item For every odd prime $p$, the inclusion
      \[
      K_{p+1,2p-1}\hookrightarrow K_{2p-1,2p-1}
      \]
      annihilates $[z_p^{(p)}]$. Indeed,
      $H_{p-1}(\mathbb{B}_pK_{2p-1,2p-1};\mathbb{Z})$ has no $p$-primary torsion.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoreme-1 -->
<!-- observation-1: body_md -->
\label{obs:top}
The weight-$n$ part of $\widetilde{S}(\Gamma)$ vanishes in degrees $>n$, so $H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)=0$
for $i>n$, and $H_n(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ is a subgroup of a free abelian group and hence
torsion-free.  Consequently, torsion in $H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ requires $n\ge i+1$.
<!-- end observation-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:KP}
For every finite graph $\Gamma$ and every $n$, the torsion of $H_1(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ is a
direct sum of copies of $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:topcycle}
Write $\mathrm{rest}=(v_2,e_2),\dots,(v_m,e_m)$.  A top chain $f$ is a cycle if and only
if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
\item if $e=vx$ and $x$ is occupied, then $f((v,e),\mathrm{rest})=0$;
\item if $e=vx$ and neither $v$ nor $x$ is occupied by $\mathrm{rest}$, then
      $f((v,e),\mathrm{rest})=-f((x,e),\mathrm{rest})$.
\end{enumerate}
A cycle moreover satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*,resume]
\item $f$ vanishes unless $e_1,\dots,e_m$ are pairwise disjoint and each $e_i$ points to
      an unoccupied vertex.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Conditions (a) and (b) say that \eqref{eq:dtop} vanishes: in (a) the sum has one term,
in (b) two.

For (c), suppose $e_1=vx$ and $e_2=yx$.  By (a) we may assume $x$ is unoccupied.  Moving
particle $1$ to $x$ by (b) produces a tuple in which particle $2$ points to the
occupied vertex $x$, and this value is $0$ by (a).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:Zcycles}
For a simple graph $\Gamma$, $H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;R)$ is isomorphic to the module of
functions $F$ on ordered oriented $m$-matchings of $\Gamma$ which are alternating,
odd under reversal of an edge, and satisfy \eqref{eq:Z} for every ordered
$(m-1)$-matching $M'$ and every vertex $v\notin V(M')$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By Observation~\ref{obs:top} there are no chains above degree $m$, so
$H_m=\ker\partial_m$.  Conversely, any such $F$, extended by zero to tuples that are not
matchings or point to occupied vertices, satisfies (a), (b) and the sum-zero conditions.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:C3}
For $\Gamma=C_3$ and $m=1$, \eqref{eq:Z} at $v$ reads $F(vx)+F(vy)=0$, and oddness gives
$F(xv)=-F(vx)$.  The solutions are the multiples of the cyclic orientation, so
$H_1(\mathbb{B}_1C_3;R)\cong R$, as it should be.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:top}
For every commutative ring $R$,
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};R)\cong\ker\Bigl(U_{r-1}\colon R^{\binom{[N]}{r-1}}\to R^{\binom{[N]}{r}}\Bigr),
\qquad N=m+r-1 .
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For $r=0$ there are no $m$-matchings, so every top cycle vanishes by
Lemma~\ref{lem:topcycle}(c), and both sides are zero.  Let $r\ge1$.
Let $M'$ be an $(m-1)$-matching.  It leaves two free vertices $a,a'\in A$ and a set
$B'\subset B$ of $r$ free vertices.  Since edges are oriented from $A$ to $B$, the
conditions \eqref{eq:Z} become:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item[(R1)] at $v=b\in B'$: $-F(ab,M')-F(a'b,M')=0$, i.e.\ $F(ab,M')+F(a'b,M')=0$;
\item[(R2)] at $v=a\in\{a,a'\}$: $\sum_{b\in B'}F(ab,M')=0$.
\end{itemize}
An $m$-matching is described by three pieces of data: its free $A$-vertex $\alpha$, its
free $(r-1)$-subset $\beta\in\binom{[N]}{r-1}$, and a bijection $\sigma\colon A\setminus\alpha\to B\setminus\beta$.
Order $A=\{a_1<\dots<a_{m+1}\}$ and put $p(a_i)=i$.  Let $G(\alpha,\beta,\sigma)$ be the value
of $F$ with edges listed in increasing order of their $A$-endpoints.

\emph{Step 1.}  For $ab,cd\in M$, three applications of (R1), cycling the free
$A$-vertex $\alpha\to a\to c\to\alpha$, followed by one transposition, give
\[
F(ab,cd,\dots)=-F(\alpha b,cd,\dots)=F(\alpha b,ad,\dots)=-F(cb,ad,\dots)=F(ad,cb,\dots).
\]
Hence $G$ is invariant under $\sigma\mapsto\sigma\circ(a\ c)$, and therefore
$G=g(\alpha,\beta)$ does not depend on $\sigma$.  (For $m=1$ there is nothing to prove:
$\sigma$ is the unique map between two singletons.)

\emph{Step 2.}  In (R1) the edge at $a$ moves to $\alpha$.  Restoring increasing order
moves it past the $|p(a)-p(\alpha)|-1$ vertices strictly between them, so
$(-1)^{p(\alpha)}g(\alpha,\beta)=(-1)^{p(a)}g(a,\beta)$.  Hence
$g(\alpha,\beta)=(-1)^{p(\alpha)}h(\beta)$ for a function $h\colon\binom{[N]}{r-1}\to R$.

\emph{Step 3.}  The $r$ terms of (R2) have the same $\alpha$ and the same order of
$A$-endpoints, and their free $(r-1)$-subsets are the $(r-1)$-subsets $B'\setminus b$ of $B'$.
So (R2) says $(U_{r-1}h)(B')=0$.  Every $r$-subset $T$ of $B$ occurs as some $B'$: match
the $m-1$ vertices of $A\setminus\{a,a'\}$ bijectively onto $B\setminus T$, which has
$m-1$ elements.

\emph{Step 4.}  Conversely, for $h\in\ker U_{r-1}$, the function $G=(-1)^{p(\alpha)}h(\beta)$
satisfies (R1) by Step~2 and (R2) by Step~3.  Every vertex not in $V(M')$ lies in
$\{a,a'\}\cup B'$, so these are all the conditions \eqref{eq:Z}.  The theorem follows
from Proposition~\ref{prop:Zcycles}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:identity}
$D_{j+1}U_j-U_{j-1}D_j=(N-2j)\,\mathrm{id}$ on $R^{\binom{[N]}{j}}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For $|S|=j$, $(D_{j+1}U_jh)(S)=(N-j)h(S)+\sum_{|S\cap S'|=j-1}h(S')$, since each $S'$
with $|S\cap S'|=j-1$ lies in exactly one $(j+1)$-set containing $S$, namely $S\cup S'$.
Similarly $(U_{j-1}D_jh)(S)=j\,h(S)+\sum_{|S\cap S'|=j-1}h(S')$.  Subtract.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:kerU}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item If $N>2j$, then $\ker(U_j\colon\mathbb{Z}^{\binom{[N]}{j}}\to\mathbb{Z}^{\binom{[N]}{j+1}})=0$.
\item The constant function $1$ satisfies $U_j1=(j+1)\cdot1$.  Hence, if $j+1=p$ is
      prime, $1\in\ker(U_j\otimes\mathbb{F}_p)$.
\item If $j+1=p$ is prime and $N\ge2p-1$, then $\ker(U_j\otimes\mathbb{F}_p)$ is one-dimensional,
      spanned by the constant function.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
(1) Let $U_jh=0$ with $h$ integral.  Taking the standard inner product with $h$ in
Lemma~\ref{lem:identity},
\[
0=\langle D_{j+1}U_jh,h\rangle=\langle U_{j-1}D_jh,h\rangle+(N-2j)\|h\|^2=\|D_jh\|^2+(N-2j)\|h\|^2,
\]
using that $D_j$ is the transpose of $U_{j-1}$.  Since $N>2j$, $h=0$.

(2) Every $(j+1)$-set has $j+1$ subsets of size $j$.

(3) By Wilson's rank formula \cite{Wilson}, for $t\le\min(k,N-k)$ the rank
of the inclusion matrix $W_{t,k}(N)$ of $t$-subsets versus $k$-subsets of an $N$-set over
$\mathbb{F}_p$ is
\[
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_p}W_{t,k}(N)=\sum_{i\colon\ p\nmid\binom{k-i}{t-i}}\Bigl[\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1}\Bigr].
\]
Here $t=j=p-1$, $k=p$ and $N\ge2p-1$, so $N-k\ge t$ and the formula applies;
$\binom{k-i}{t-i}=p-i$ is divisible by $p$ only for $i=0$.  Hence
$\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_p}U_j=\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\bigl[\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1}\bigr]=\binom N{p-1}-1$, and the
kernel is one-dimensional.  By (2) it is spanned by the constant.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:allprimes}
Let $m\ge2$ and $r\ge2$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item If $m\ge r$, then $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})=0$.
\item Let $p$ be a prime and $m\ge p$.  Then $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+p-1};\mathbb{F}_p)\cong\mathbb{F}_p$,
      spanned by the class of the constant function, and the $p$-primary part of
      $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+p-1};\mathbb{Z})$ is a nonzero cyclic group.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
(1) is Theorem~\ref{thm:top} with Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(1), since $N=m+r-1>2(r-1)$.

(2) Put $r=p$; then $m\ge p=r$, so $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z})=0$ by (1), and $N=m+r-1\ge2p-1$.
By the universal coefficient theorem, $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{F}_p)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(H_{m-1}(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z}),\mathbb{F}_p)$,
whose dimension is the number of $p$-primary cyclic summands of $H_{m-1}$.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:top} and Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(3), this dimension is exactly $1$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
$H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,3})$ and $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,4})$ contain $\mathbb{Z}/2$; $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5})$ contains $\mathbb{Z}/3$;
$H_4(\mathbb{B}_5K_{6,9})$ contains $\mathbb{Z}/5$; $H_6(\mathbb{B}_7K_{8,13})$ contains $\mathbb{Z}/7$.  In general the
first $p$-torsion produced by the corollary lives in $H_{p-1}(\mathbb{B}_pK_{p+1,2p-1})$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:wilson}
Let $0\le t\le k$ and $N\ge t+k$.  The inclusion matrix $W_{t,k}(N)$, with rows indexed
by $t$-subsets and columns by $k$-subsets, is equivalent over $\mathbb{Z}$ to a rectangular
diagonal matrix with nonzero entries
\[
\binom{k-i}{t-i}\quad\text{of multiplicity}\quad\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1},\qquad 0\le i\le t.
\]
Here equivalence means multiplication by unimodular integer matrices on the left and
right, and the entries are listed without regard to divisibility.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:exacttors}
Let $m\ge1$ and $r\ge0$, put $N=m+r-1$, $s=\min\{m,r\}$, $b=\binom N{r-1}-\binom N{s-1}$ and
$\mu_j=\binom N{s-j}-\binom N{s-j-1}$, and let $K=K_{m+1,m+r-1}$.  For every commutative
ring $R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:topR}
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;R)\;\cong\;\ker(U_{r-1}\otimes R)\;\cong\;R^{b}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=2}^{s}R[j]^{\mu_j},
\qquad R[j]=\{x\in R: jx=0\},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:torsformula}
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})\;\cong\;\operatorname{Tors}\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{j=2}^{s}\bigl(\mathbb{Z}/j\bigr)^{\mu_j} .
\end{equation}
In particular the integral top homology is free of rank $b$.  It vanishes if and only if $m\ge r$: for $m<r$ one has $s=m$ and
$b=\binom Nm-\binom N{m-1}>0$ since $m\le N/2$, and for $r=m+1$ this is the Catalan number
$\frac1{m+1}\binom{2m}m$.  In particular, for $m\ge r$ the torsion formula is
\[
\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-2}\bigl(\mathbb{Z}/(r-i)\bigr)^{\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1}} .
\]
For a prime power $q=p^a$ and $r=q$, the $p$-primary part has exactly one cyclic
summand of order $q$ and all its other cyclic summands have order at most $p^{a-1}$ if
$m\ge q$; it has exponent less than $q$ if $m<q$.  For $a=1$: the $p$-primary part is
$\mathbb{Z}/p$ if $m\ge p$ and is zero if $m<p$.  (For $m=1$ the sum in \eqref{eq:torsformula}
is empty, and indeed $H_0$ is free.  For $r\in\{0,1\}$ one has $s=r\le1$, $b=0$
and empty sums: the top homology vanishes and $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})$ is
torsion-free.)
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $r=0$ the matrix $U_{r-1}$ is empty, both sides of \eqref{eq:topR} are zero by
Theorem~\ref{thm:top}, and the universal coefficient argument below gives
$\operatorname{Tor}(H_{m-1},\mathbb{Z}/\ell^a)=0$ for all $\ell,a$, so $H_{m-1}$ is torsion-free.  Let
$r\ge1$.  If $m\ge r$, the transpose of $U_{r-1}$ is $W_{r-1,r}(N)$ and Wilson's hypothesis is
$N\ge2r-1$ (for $r=1$ this is $W_{0,1}(N)$, a row of ones, with $N=m\ge1$).  If $m<r$, complementing all subsets identifies $U_{r-1}$, up to row and
column permutations, with $W_{m-1,m}(N)$, and its hypothesis is $N\ge2m-1$.  Both hold in
the respective ranges.  Consequently the nonzero diagonal entries of $U_{r-1}$ are
\[
d_i=s-i\quad\text{with multiplicity}\quad\nu_i=\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1},\qquad 0\le i\le s-1.
\]
Their multiplicities sum to $\binom N{s-1}$, so $U_{r-1}$ has $b=\binom N{r-1}-\binom N{s-1}$
zero columns in diagonal form.  Since unimodular matrices stay invertible over every
$R$, the kernel of $U_{r-1}\otimes R$ is that of the diagonal matrix, namely
$R^b\oplus\bigoplus_iR[d_i]^{\nu_i}$; with Theorem~\ref{thm:top} and $j=s-i$ this is
\eqref{eq:topR}.  For $R=\mathbb{Z}$ all $R[d_i]$ vanish, proving the assertion about the
integral top homology.

Put $G=H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$.  For a prime $\ell$ and $a\ge1$, take $R=\mathbb{Z}/\ell^a$.  The
split universal coefficient sequence and \eqref{eq:topR} give isomorphisms of finite
abelian groups
\[
R^b\oplus\operatorname{Tor}(G,R)\;\cong\;H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;R)\;\cong\;R^b\oplus\bigoplus_{i=0}^{s-1}R[d_i]^{\nu_i}.
\]
Cancellation of the common finite summand $R^b$ is valid
by the classification of finite abelian groups.  As
\[
R[d_i]\cong\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{\min\{a,v_\ell(d_i)\}},
\]
comparison for all $\ell$ and $a$ determines every elementary divisor of $\operatorname{Tors} G$.  The
result is the direct sum of the $\mathbb{Z}/d_i$ with the stated multiplicities; the entries
$d_{s-1}=1$ contribute nothing.  This also equals the torsion of $\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}$.  Its
possible free summand has no effect on this argument.  Reindexing by $j=s-i$ gives
\eqref{eq:torsformula}.

When $r=q$ and $m\ge q$, the diagonal entries are $d_i=q-i$, $0\le i\le q-1$; only
$d_0=q$ has $p$-adic valuation $a$, with $\nu_0=1$, while $v_p(q-i)=v_p(i)\le a-1$ for
$1\le i\le q-1$.  When $m<q$, all diagonal entries are at most $m<q$, so their $p$-parts
are at most $p^{a-1}$.  This proves the final assertions.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:primary}
In the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors},
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_\ell H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})\cong\bigoplus_{a\ge1}\bigl(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^a\bigr)^{M_{\ell,a}},\qquad
M_{\ell,a}=\sum_{\substack{2\le j\le s\\ v_\ell(j)=a}}\Bigl[\binom N{s-j}-\binom N{s-j-1}\Bigr].
\]
The exponent of the torsion subgroup is $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,s)$.  Its prime
divisors are exactly the primes at most $s$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Decompose each cyclic group in \eqref{eq:torsformula} into primary factors.  All
displayed multiplicities are positive because $0\le s-j\le s-2<N/2$.  Thus each order
$2,\dots,s$ occurs, giving the exponent and the set of prime divisors.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:orderk}
Let $m\ge1$, $r\ge0$, $k\ge2$, and $K=K_{m+1,m+r-1}$.  The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$ has an element of order $k$.
\item $\mathbb{Z}/k$ is a direct summand of $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$.
\item $q(k)\le\min\{m,r\}$, i.e.\ $m\ge q(k)$ and $r\ge q(k)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular $H_{q-1}(\mathbb{B}_qK_{q+1,2q-1};\mathbb{Z})$ has a direct summand $\mathbb{Z}/k$ for $q=q(k)$,
and $(q,q)$ is the least pair $(m,r)$ in the coordinatewise order for which
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})$ contains an element of order $k$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Put $s=\min\{m,r\}$ and write
$G=\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})\cong\bigoplus_{j=2}^s(\mathbb{Z}/j)^{\mu_j}$ with all $\mu_j>0$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:primary}).  An element of order $k$ exists in a finite abelian group
if and only if, for each $i$, some cyclic summand has order divisible by $p_i^{a_i}$.
Since the cyclic summands of $G$ have orders exactly $2,\dots,s$, such a summand exists
if and only if $p_i^{a_i}\le s$.  Hence (1) is equivalent to $\max_ip_i^{a_i}\le s$,
which is (3).  If (3) holds, choose one cyclic summand from the term
$j=p_i^{a_i}$ for each $i$. These terms are distinct, and the selected summands give
$\mathbb{Z}/p_1^{a_1}\oplus\dots\oplus\mathbb{Z}/p_t^{a_t}\cong\mathbb{Z}/k$ as a direct summand of $G$,
giving (2); and (2) trivially implies (1).
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:orderk}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item Since $k\mid\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,s)$ if and only if $q(k)\le s$, condition
      (3) can be restated as $k\mid\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,\min\{m,r\})$, in
      accordance with the exponent computed in Corollary~\ref{cor:primary}.  For
      $r\ge m$ every generalized theta class has order exactly
      $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,m)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:torsgen}), so a suitable multiple
      of a single explicit class realizes every order $k$ with $q(k)\le m$.
\item For example, $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{155}\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/2)^4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ already
      contains elements of order $6$. Within the family
      $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})$, order $12$ first occurs at $(m,r)=(4,4)$,
      in $H_3(\mathbb{B}_4K_{5,7};\mathbb{Z})$, and order $30$ at $(m,r)=(5,5)$,
      in $H_4(\mathbb{B}_5K_{6,9};\mathbb{Z})$.
\item Corollary~\ref{cor:orderk-minimal} establishes minor-minimality for arbitrary
      order $k$, using $q(k)$ as the graph parameter. Thus the occurrence criterion
      above also identifies the graphs to which the minimality theorem applies.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
For $r=2$ and $m\ge2$, the torsion is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. For $r=3$ and $m\ge3$ it is $\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{m+1}$.
For $r=4$ and $m\ge4$ it is $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/3)^{N-1}\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\binom N2-N}$, where
$N=m+3$.  For $m=5$, $r=5$,
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_4(\mathbb{B}_5K_{6,9};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/5\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/4)^8\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/3)^{27}\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{48}.
\]
The prime-to-$5$ subgroup in this example has exponent $12$, not at most $4$: bounds on
the orders of displayed cyclic summands are not bounds on the orders of all elements.
For $r=11$ and $m\ge11$, the formula also gives $(\mathbb{Z}/9)^{\binom{m+10}2-(m+10)}$ as a
direct summand.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
This argument determines the free rank of $H_m$, not of $H_{m-1}$.  The latter still
depends on lower Betti numbers through Gal's formula.  For $m=3$ the known $H_1$ suffices
in the cases below; see Corollary~\ref{cor:small-cases}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:T}
For $N\ge5$ and every commutative ring $R$,
\[
T_R(N)\cong R[6]\oplus R[2]^{\,N-2}.
\]
In particular $T_\mathbb{Z}(N)=0$, $T_{\mathbb{F}_3}(N)\cong\mathbb{F}_3$ (the constants), $T_{\mathbb{F}_2}(N)\cong\mathbb{F}_2^{N-1}$,
$T_{\mathbb{F}_p}(N)=0$ for $p\ge5$, $T_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(N)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{N-1}$ and $T_{\mathbb{Z}/9}(N)\cong\mathbb{Z}/3$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Write $B=\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}$ and $x_i=h(0i)$ for $i\ge1$.  The triangle relation for
$\{0,i,j\}$ gives $h(ij)=-x_i-x_j$, and then the relation for $\{i,j,k\}$ with
$i,j,k\ge1$ reads $2(x_i+x_j+x_k)=0$.  These are all the relations.  Since $N-1\ge4$,
comparing the relations for $\{i,j,k\}$ and $\{i,j,l\}$ gives $2x_k=2x_l$ for all $k,l$.
Put $a=x_1$ and $b_i=x_i-a$ for $2\le i\le N-1$.  Then $2b_i=0$, and the relations become
$6a=0$.  Conversely $6a=0$ and $2b_i=0$ imply all triangle relations.  This gives the
isomorphism, with $a\in R[6]$ and $(b_2,\dots,b_{N-1})\in R[2]^{N-2}$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:exact}
For every $m\ge3$ (this is Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} for $r=3$; we give the direct
argument),
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+2};\mathbb{Z})=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+2};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{m+1}.
\]
For $m=2$, $H_2(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,4})\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The vanishing is Corollary~\ref{cor:allprimes}(1).  Since $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z})=0$, the
universal coefficient theorem gives $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(H_{m-1},\mathbb{Z}/q)$ for every
$q$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:top} with Lemma~\ref{lem:T} ($N=m+2\ge5$) computes the left
side:
\begin{itemize}
\item $q=p\ge5$ prime: $0$, so there is no $p$-torsion;
\item $q=3$: $\mathbb{F}_3$, so there is exactly one $3$-primary cyclic summand $\mathbb{Z}/3^a$;
\item $q=9$: $\mathbb{Z}/3$.  Since $\operatorname{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/3^a,\mathbb{Z}/9)$ has order $\min(3^a,9)$, we get $a=1$;
\item $q=2$: $\mathbb{F}_2^{m+1}$, so there are exactly $m+1$ cyclic summands $\mathbb{Z}/2^{a_i}$;
\item $q=4$: $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{m+1}$, of order $2^{m+1}$.  Since $\operatorname{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/2^{a_i},\mathbb{Z}/4)$ has order
      $\min(2^{a_i},4)\ge2$, all $a_i=1$.
\end{itemize}
For $m=2$, $N=4$: the relations $2(x_i+x_j+x_k)=0$ involve only the single triple
$\{1,2,3\}$, and over $\mathbb{Z}$ the solution set of $x_1+x_2+x_3=0$ is $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:r2}
For every $m\ge2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} for $r=2$), $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+1};R)\cong R[2]$
for every commutative ring $R$, and
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+1};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2 .
\]
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The kernel of $U_1$ consists of the functions $h$ on $B$ with $h(x)+h(y)=0$ for all
$x\ne y$.  Since $|B|=m+1\ge3$, for distinct $x,y,z$ we get $h(x)=-h(y)=h(z)=-h(x)$, so
$h$ is constant with $2h=0$; conversely such $h$ lie in the kernel.  Thus
$\ker U_1\cong R[2]$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:top} gives the first claim.  The second
follows as in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:exact}: $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z})=0$ since
$R[2]=0$ for $R=\mathbb{Z}$; $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{F}_2)\cong\mathbb{F}_2$ gives exactly one $2$-primary
summand and $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z}/4)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ gives exponent one; and
$H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{F}_p)=0$ for odd $p$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:ko-park}
For $m=2$, Corollary~\ref{cor:r2} says $\operatorname{Tors} H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,3})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:subgraph} with $p=m=2$ says that no proper subgraph of $K_{3,3}$ has
$2$-torsion in $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2)$.  Both are special cases of Theorem~\ref{thm:KP} in the
form of \cite{KP}: $H_1(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$, for $n\ge2$, has $2$-torsion exactly when $\Gamma$ is
non-planar, and $K_{3,3}$ is a minimal non-planar graph.  Thus the top-homology method
recovers this part of the Ko--Park theorem, and Theorems~\ref{thm:top}
and~\ref{thm:subgraph} may be viewed as its analogue for every prime.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:small-cases}
For $1\le m\le3$ and $r\ge0$, the integral homology of
$\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1}$ is given in Table~\ref{tab:small-cases},
and vanishes in degrees greater than $m$.
Here
\[
g_2(r)=\binom{r+1}2-\binom{r+1}1,\qquad
g_3(r)=\binom{r+2}3 - \binom{r+2}2,
\]
and
\[
f_3(r)=
2\binom{r+2}3 +19 \binom{r+2}2-11\binom{r+2}1
\qquad(r\ge3).
\]
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For $m=1$, the configuration space is the graph itself.
The graph $K_{2,0}$ consists of two isolated points. For every $r\ge1$,
$K_{2,r}$ is connected and has cycle rank $r-1$.
All the remaining configuration spaces are connected, so $H_0\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
Observation~\ref{obs:top} gives vanishing in degrees greater than $m$.

For $m=2$, the graphs at $r=0,1$ are the three-armed star and a
subdivision of the three-edge theta graph. The Ko--Park formula
\cite[Theorem~3.16]{KP} gives $H_1\cong\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}^3$, respectively.
For the theta graph, the cycle rank $2$ and the $2$-cut contribution
$(3-1)(3-2)/2=1$ give rank $3$.
For every $r\ge2$, $K_{3,r+1}$ is simple, $3$-connected and non-planar,
so the same formula gives
\[
H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,r+1};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2r}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2.
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:top} gives $H_2=0$ for $r=0,1$, while
Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} gives, for $r\ge2$,
\[
H_2(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,r+1};\mathbb{Z})\cong
\mathbb{Z}^{\binom{r+1}{2}-\binom{r+1}{1}}=\mathbb{Z}^{g_2(r)}.
\]

For $m=3$, Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} gives $H_3=0$ for $0\le r\le2$
and, for $r\ge3$,
\[
H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,r+2};\mathbb{Z})\cong
\mathbb{Z}^{\binom{r+2}{3}-\binom{r+2}{2}}=\mathbb{Z}^{g_3(r)}.
\]
The same theorem gives torsion-free $H_2$ for $r=0,1$,
$\operatorname{Tors} H_2\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ for $r=2$, and
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_2\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{r+1}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3
\qquad(r\ge3).
\]
For $r=0$, the graph $K_{4,2}$ is a subdivision of the four-edge
theta graph. Its cycle rank is $3$, and the $2$-cut consisting of
the two degree-$4$ vertices has four components, contributing
$(4-1)(4-2)/2=3$ to the free rank. There are no cut vertices, and
the marked components are topological circles. Thus Ko--Park gives
$H_1\cong\mathbb{Z}^6$. For every $r\ge1$, $K_{4,r+2}$ is simple,
$3$-connected and non-planar, and the same formula gives
\[
H_1(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,r+2};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{3(r+1)}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2.
\]
Gal's formula yields
\begin{align*}
\chi(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,r+2})
&=[t^3]\frac{(1-(r+1)t)^4(1-3t)^{r+2}}{(1-t)^{4(r+2)}}\\
&=\frac{r^3}{6}+\frac{21r^2}{2}+\frac{49r}{3}-4.
\end{align*}
For $r=0,1,2$ this gives $\chi=-4,23,72$, and hence
$b_2=\chi-1+b_1=1,28,80$, respectively.
For $r\ge3$, the Euler characteristic identity instead gives
\[
b_2=\chi-1+b_1+b_3
=\chi-1+3(r+1)+g_3(r)=f_3(r).
\]
Combining these ranks with the torsion calculation proves the table.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:classical-generators}
The infinite cyclic groups
\[
H_1(\mathbb{B}_1K_{2,2};\mathbb{Z}),\qquad
H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,1};\mathbb{Z}),\qquad
H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,2};\mathbb{Z})
\]
are generated, respectively, by the loop class, the star class, and the
theta class $A_2$ of An--Knudsen \cite[Construction~3.13, Lemma~3.14]{AK}.
The corresponding parameter pairs are
\[
(m,r)=(1,2),\qquad (2,0),\qquad (3,0).
\]
Section~\ref{sec:explicit} places these classical generators within the
explicit constructions of this paper.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:theta}
Let $m\ge2$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item $z_m^{(0)}$ is a cycle in $S(K_{m+1,m-1})$, and its integral
      homology class is nonzero and primitive.
\item For $m=2$, $z_2^{(0)}$ is the star class of the centre $b\in B$ and
      represents a generator of $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,1})\cong\mathbb{Z}$.  For $m=3$, $z_3^{(0)}$
      represents the theta class $\pm[A_2]$, a generator of $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,2})\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(1) Fix an $(m-2)$-matching $M''$ and write $i<j<k$ for the three
vertices of $A$ it misses. For each $b\in B\setminus V(M'')$, the
contribution to the boundary with remaining crossings $M''$ is,
up to the common sign $(-1)^{p(i)+p(j)+p(k)-3}$,
\[
\bigl(([i]-[j])([b]-[k])-([i]-[k])([b]-[j])
      +([j]-[k])([b]-[i])\bigr)\gamma_{M''}=0.
\]
The differentiated crossing has position $p(k)-2$, $p(j)-1$,
or $p(i)$ in the respective products. All resting factors have
degree zero, so the displayed cancellation is literal. These are
all boundary terms.

To prove primitivity, use the coefficient projections \eqref{eq:explode} defined above. Enumerate $B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_{m-1}\}$ and choose distinct
$a_1,\ldots,a_{m-1}\in A$. Explode $b_1,\ldots,b_{m-1}$ successively,
taking at each step the component for the half-edge of $a_jb_j$ at $b_j$.
Only terms whose crossings are precisely these $m-1$ edges survive.
The image of $z_m^{(0)}$ is therefore
$\pm([a_m]-[a_{m+1}])$ in $H_0(\mathbb{B}_1\Gamma_B;\mathbb{Z})$, where $a_m,a_{m+1}$
are the two remaining vertices of $A$. The graph $\Gamma_B$ is the
disjoint union of $m+1$ stars, one centered at each vertex of $A$.
This difference is primitive in its free zeroth homology.
Consequently $[z_m^{(0)}]$ is nonzero and primitive over $\mathbb{Z}$.

(2) For $m=2$, $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,1})$ is infinite cyclic, generated by the star
class. For $m=3$, subdivision invariance and \cite[Lemma~3.14]{AK}
identify $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,2})$ with the infinite cyclic group generated
by $[A_2]$. Primitivity proves the claimed identifications, up to orientation.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:thetacoef}
Let $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ in $K=K_{m+1,m-1}$, $m\ge2$.  The component of
$\pi_a(z_m^{(0)})$ at the half-edge $h_{a,ab}$ is
$(-1)^{p(a)-1}\,z_{m-1}^{(0)}$, where $z_{m-1}^{(0)}$ is formed on the complete
bipartite graph $K_{A\setminus a,\,B\setminus b}\cong K_{m,m-2}$ with the induced
order of $A\setminus a$, and is regarded as a chain of $K_a$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The half-edge $h_{a,ab}$ occurs in \eqref{eq:zm} only through the factor
$\gamma_{ab}=h_{a,ab}-h_{b,ab}$ of the terms with $a\in D=A\setminus\{i,k\}$ and
$\varphi(a)=b$; the remaining factors are $([a_i]-[a_k])\prod_{d\in D\setminus a}\gamma_{d\varphi(d)}$
with $\varphi|_{D\setminus a}$ a bijection onto $B\setminus b$.  Moving $\gamma_{ab}$ to
the front passes the $\#\{d\in D: d<a\}=p(a)-1-[i<a]-[k<a]$ factors before it.  Let
$p'$ be the position in $A\setminus a$; then $p'(x)=p(x)-[x>a]$ and hence
$(-1)^{p(x)+[x<a]}=-(-1)^{p'(x)}$ for $x\ne a$.  The total sign is therefore
$(-1)^{p(a)-1}(-1)^{p'(i)+p'(k)}$, and the sum over $i<k$ in $A\setminus a$ and over
the bijections $D\setminus a\to B\setminus b$ is $z_{m-1}^{(0)}$ on
$K_{A\setminus a,B\setminus b}$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:thetanonzero}
For every $m\ge2$ and $k\ge0$, the extension by zero of $z_m^{(0)}$ to
$K_{m+1,m-1+k}$ represents a nonzero class in $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m-1+k};\mathbb{F}_2)$.
Consequently $A_{m-1}=[z_m^{(0)}]\ne0$ in $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m-1};\mathbb{Z})$, it is not
divisible by $2$, and it stays nonzero under every inclusion
$K_{m+1,m-1}\subseteq K_{m+1,m-1+k}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Induction on $m$, for all $k$ simultaneously.  Let $\Gamma=K_{m+1,m-1+k}$ with parts
$A$ and $B$, let $B_0\subset B$ be the $(m-1)$-subset on which $z_m^{(0)}$ is formed,
and let $a\in A$.  Then $\Gamma_a$ is $K_{A\setminus a,B}\cong K_{m,m-1+k}$ with one
pendant edge attached at each vertex of $B$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:thetacoef}, applied to
the chain $z_m^{(0)}$ on $K_{A,B_0}$, shows that the component of
$\pi_a(z_m^{(0)})$ at $h_{a,ab}$, $b\in B_0$, is $\pm z_{m-1}^{(0)}$ formed on
$K_{A\setminus a,B_0\setminus b}$, that is, the extension by zero of $z_{m-1}^{(0)}$
to $K_{A\setminus a,B}\cong K_{m,(m-1)-1+(k+1)}$, regarded as a chain of $\Gamma_a$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:pendant}, applied with $\mathbb{F}_2$ coefficients and iterated over the
pendant edges, $H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}K_{A\setminus a,B};\mathbb{F}_2)$ is a direct summand of
$H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_a;\mathbb{F}_2)$.  Hence, if the statement holds for $(m-1,k+1)$, the
image of $[z_m^{(0)}]$ under $\pi_{a*}$ is nonzero, and so is $[z_m^{(0)}]$.

It remains to treat $m=2$, where $z_2^{(0)}$ is the star class $\sigma_b$ of the
vertex $b\in B$ of degree $3$ in $K_{3,1+k}$.  Note that a chain which is a boundary
in $K_{3,1+k}$ is a boundary in every larger $K_{3,1+k'}$, so it suffices to treat
$k\ge2$.  Then $K_{3,1+k}$ is $3$-connected and non-planar; by Ko--Park
\cite[Theorem~3.16]{KP}, $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,1+k})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{\beta_1}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, and the
element of order $2$ is represented by the star class of any vertex of degree at least
$3$ \cite[Theorem~3.16]{KP}, \cite[Lemma~C.4]{ADK}.  In particular $\sigma_b$ is nonzero modulo $2$.  (For
$k=0$ one can also explode $b$: $\Gamma_b$ is three disjoint arcs, and the component
of $\pi_b(\sigma_b)$ at $h_{b,a_jb}$ is $\pm([a_i]-[a_k])\ne0$ in $H_0(\mathbb{B}_1\Gamma_b)$;
this also shows that $\sigma_b$ is primitive.)
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:universal}
For every $h\colon\binom B{r-1}\to R$,
\[
\partial c_h=z_{U_{r-1}h},\qquad (U_{r-1}h)(T)=\sum_{b\in T}h(T\setminus b).
\]
Consequently $c_h$ is a cycle if and only if $U_{r-1}h=0$, and in that case $c_h$ is
the top cycle corresponding to $h$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:top}: its matching function
in the sense of Proposition~\ref{prop:Zcycles}, read off as the coefficient of the
monomial of half-edges at the tails, is $(-1)^{p(\alpha)}h(\beta)$, the function of
Step~4 in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:top}.  In particular every top cycle of
$K$ over $R$ is of the form $c_h$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
In a matching with free $A$-vertex $\alpha$, the crossing at $a$
occupies position $p(a)-[\alpha<a]$. Differentiating that factor gives
$[b]-[a]$ with sign $(-1)^{p(a)-[\alpha<a]-1}$.  A face with a
particle resting at $b\in B$ arises from the two matchings $M'\cup\{ab\}$ and
$M'\cup\{a'b\}$; they have the same free $B$-set, hence the same weight $h(\beta)$,
and their signs differ by $[a'<a]-[a<a']=\pm1$, so they cancel.  A face with a particle resting at
$a\in A$ and crossings $M'$ arises from the matchings $M'\cup\{ab\}$, where $b$ runs
over the $r$ free vertices $B'=B\setminus V(M')$; the matching $M'\cup\{ab\}$ has
free $B$-set $B'\setminus b$, so the face occurs with total coefficient
$\sum_{b\in B'}h(B'\setminus b)=(U_{r-1}h)(B')$ times $(-1)^{p(\alpha)+p(a)-[\alpha<a]}$, where $\alpha$
is the other free $A$-vertex. For $a<\alpha$ this is the coefficient
of $[a]$ in the pair $\{a,\alpha\}$ of \eqref{eq:zm}; for $a>\alpha$
it has the opposite sign. Thus it is the sign of the corresponding term of $z_m^{(0)}|_{V(M')\cap B}=z_{\delta_{B'}}$.
Summing over $B'$ gives $\partial c_h=z_{U_{r-1}h}$.  The remaining assertions follow
from $z_g=0\Leftrightarrow g=0$ and from Theorem~\ref{thm:top}, whose proof
identifies the top cycles with the functions $(-1)^{p(\alpha)}h(\beta)$,
$h\in\ker U_{r-1}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:cubes}
For all $m\ge1$ and $r\ge0$, $\partial w_m=r\,z_m$ in $S(K_{m+1,m+r-1})$.  (For
$r=0$ both sides are zero, since there are no $m$-matchings; for $r=1$ the formula
reads $\partial w_m=z_m$.)
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For $r\ge1$, take $h\equiv1$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:universal};
then $U_{r-1}h=r\cdot1$. For $r=0$, there are no $m$-matchings
and both sides are zero.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:explicitgen}
Let $q\ge2$, $m\ge q$, and set $r=q$. Then $[z_m^{(q)}]\in H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+q-1};\mathbb{Z})$ has order
exactly $q$.  For prime $q=p$, it generates the entire $p$-primary part $\mathbb{Z}/p$.  For a
prime power $q=p^a$, it generates a cyclic direct summand of order $q$ in the $p$-primary
part.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:cubes} gives $\partial w_m=qz_m$.  Since the chain groups are free,
$q\,\partial z_m=0$ implies $\partial z_m=0$.  The reduction $\bar w_m$ is a cycle with
coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/q$.  Its coefficient at $h_{a_2,a_2b_1}\cdots h_{a_{m+1},a_{m+1}b_m}$
is $-1$, so this chain has order exactly $q$.  There are no chains above degree $m$, and
hence its homology class also has order $q$.

Since $m\ge r$, the integral top group is zero.  In the coefficient sequence
$0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\,q\,}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/q\to0$, the Bockstein
\[
\beta_q\colon H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z}/q)\longrightarrow H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})
\]
is therefore injective and sends $[\bar w_m]$ to $[z_m]$.  This proves the exact order.
When $q=p$ is prime, the entire $p$-primary part is $\mathbb{Z}/p$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors}.  When $q=p^a$, that theorem gives exactly one summand
$\mathbb{Z}/p^a$ and all other $p$-primary summands of exponent at most $p^{a-1}$.  An element of
order $p^a$ has unit coordinate in the first summand; its cyclic subgroup is consequently
a direct summand.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
In the identification of Theorem~\ref{thm:top}, $\bar w_m$ corresponds to the constant
function $h\equiv1$.  In the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:cubes}, the cancelling faces
are relation (R1), and the faces of multiplicity $r$ are the relation
$U_{r-1}1=r\cdot1$.  For $m=3$, $r=3$ the cycle is
\[
z_3=\sum_{1\le i<k\le4}(-1)^{i+k}\bigl([a_i]-[a_k]\bigr)\sum_{b\ne b'}\gamma_{a_jb}\gamma_{a_lb'},\qquad\{j<l\}=\{1,2,3,4\}\setminus\{i,k\}.
\]
It consists of $240$ squares; the chain $w_3$ consists of $240$ cubes.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:wT}
For every $T\in\binom Bm$, $\ \partial w_T=\sum_{b\in T}z_m^{(0)}|_{T\setminus b}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Take $h=\delta_{B\setminus T}$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:universal}.
Its image under $U_{r-1}$ is the sum of the indicators indexed by
$(B\setminus T)\cup\{b\}$, $b\in T$, giving the assertion.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:thetatorsion}
Let $m\ge2$, $r\ge m$, $N=m+r-1$, $H=H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})$, and put
$x_{B'}=[z_m^{(0)}|_{B'}]\in H$ for $B'\in\binom B{m-1}$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item For every $T\in\binom Bm$, $\sum_{B'\subset T}x_{B'}=0$.  That is, the vector
      $(x_{B'})_{B'}$ lies in $\ker\bigl(U_{m-1}(N)\otimes H\bigr)$.
\item Every $x_{B'}$ is a torsion element, of order dividing $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,m)$.
\item Let $m=p$ be prime and $r=p$, so that $K=K_{p+1,2p-1}$ and the $p$-primary
      part of $H$ is $\mathbb{Z}/p$, generated by $[z_p]$ (Theorems~\ref{thm:exacttors}
      and~\ref{thm:explicitgen}).  Then the $p$-primary component of $x_{B'}$ is
      $[z_p]$ for every $B'$.  If $p$ is odd, the $2$-primary component of $x_{B'}$
      is also nonzero, so the order of $x_{B'}$ is divisible by $2p$.
\item In particular, in $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,3})$ the star class of every vertex of $B$ is
      the element of order $2$, and in
      $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{155}\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/2)^4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ the theta class
      $x_{B'}$ has order exactly $6$ for every $B'$, and all the $x_{B'}$ are
      congruent to $[z_3]$ modulo $2$-torsion.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
(1) is Lemma~\ref{lem:wT}.

(2) Since $N\ge2m-1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:wilson} applies to $U_{m-1}(N)=W_{m-1,m}(N)^{\mathsf T}$:
there are unimodular $P,Q$ with $U_{m-1}(N)=PDQ$, where $D$ is rectangular diagonal
with nonzero entries $d_i=m-i$ of multiplicity $\nu_i=\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1}$,
$0\le i\le m-1$, and $\sum_i\nu_i=\binom N{m-1}$ is the number of columns.  Hence
$\ker(U_{m-1}(N)\otimes H)=Q^{-1}\ker(D\otimes H)$ and
$\ker(D\otimes H)=\bigoplus_iH[d_i]^{\nu_i}$.  Every coordinate of a vector in the
kernel is an integral combination of elements killed by some $d_i\le m$, hence is
killed by $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,m)$.

(3) Write $H=F\oplus\bigoplus_\ell H_{(\ell)}$ with $F$ free and $H_{(\ell)}$ the
$\ell$-primary parts, and decompose the kernel accordingly.  Since $U_{m-1}(N)$ is
injective over $\mathbb{Z}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(1), as $N>2(m-1)$), the $F$-component of
$(x_{B'})$ vanishes; this is (2) again.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors},
$H_{(p)}\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(3), $\ker(U_{p-1}(2p-1)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/p)$
is spanned by the constant vector.  So the $p$-primary components of all $x_{B'}$ are
equal to one element $c\in H_{(p)}$.  Summing \eqref{eq:zsum} in homology,
$[z_p]=\sum_{B'}x_{B'}$, whose $p$-primary component is $\binom{2p-1}{p-1}c=c$,
because $\binom{2p-1}{p-1}\equiv\binom10\binom{p-1}{p-1}=1\pmod p$ by Lucas' theorem.
Hence $c=[z_p]$.  For the $2$-primary component, Theorem~\ref{thm:thetanonzero} with
$k=r$ shows that $x_{B'}$ is nonzero in $H\otimes\mathbb{F}_2$, i.e.\ $x_{B'}\notin2H$;
since $x_{B'}$ is torsion, its $2$-primary component is nonzero.

(4) For $K_{3,3}$, $B'=\{b\}$ and $x_{B'}$ is the star class $\sigma_b$; by (3) its
$2$-primary component is $[z_2]$, the generator of $\operatorname{Tors} H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_{3,3})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$,
and there is no other torsion, so $\sigma_b=[z_2]$.  For $K_{4,5}$, (2) and (3) give
$6x_{B'}=0$ and $2p=6\mid\operatorname{ord}(x_{B'})$.  The torsion subgroup is
$(\mathbb{Z}/2)^4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:exact}), so $x_{B'}-[z_3]$ is $2$-torsion.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:inspiration}
Theorem~\ref{thm:thetatorsion} is how the torsion cycles of this paper were found.
The theta class $A_2$ has infinite order in the subdivision $K_{4,2}$ of
$\Theta_4$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:theta}. It retains infinite order in
$K_{4,3}$ and $K_{4,4}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:theta-injective} and
Remark~\ref{rem:lowr}.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:thetatorsion},
it becomes a class of order $6$ in $K_{4,5}$, whose $3$-primary part is exactly the $3$-torsion $[z_3]$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:explicitgen}; the star class of a degree-$3$ vertex, viewed in
$K_{3,3}$, becomes the $2$-torsion of Ko--Park.  The torsion cycles $z_m$ and the
bounding chains $w_m$ are the sums \eqref{eq:zsum} and $w_m=\sum_Tw_T$ of these
restricted classes, and Lemma~\ref{lem:wT} is the reason why the coefficient $r$
appears in $\partial w_m=rz_m$: each restricted class $z_m^{(0)}|_{B'}$ is
bounded by $\sum_{T\supset B'}w_T$ up to the other restricted classes, and $B'$ lies
in $r$ sets $T$. Theorem~\ref{thm:theta-injective} below shows that these
incidence relations are all the relations, including before the torsion range.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:theta-injective}
Let $m\ge2$, $r\ge1$, and $K=K_{m+1,m+r-1}$.
The homomorphism $\Phi$ in \eqref{eq:Phi} is injective.
Its image is the subgroup generated by the restricted theta classes, and
contains the entire torsion subgroup of $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})$.
In particular, all integral relations among these classes are generated by
\[
\sum_{B'\subset C,\ |B'|=m-1}x_{B'}=0,
\qquad C\in\binom Bm.
\]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Suppose $[z_g]=0$, and choose a chain $c\in S_m(K)_m$ with $\partial c=z_g$.
Every monomial of $c$ consists of $m$ half-edges at distinct vertices:
degree and weight are both $m$, so there are no edge variables or resting
vertices. Separate the boundary into terms containing an edge variable and
terms containing a resting vertex. The former part is zero, since $z_g$
has no edge variables.

Encode $c$ by its coefficients on ordered tuples of half-edges, as in
Section~\ref{sec:matching}, but without imposing the slot-sum equations.
The edge-variable part of the differential is still \eqref{eq:dtop}.
Its vanishing gives exactly conditions (a) and (b) of Lemma~\ref{lem:topcycle}:
a coefficient is zero if a half-edge points to another occupied vertex,
and reversing an edge whose endpoints are unoccupied by the other slots changes its sign.
The proof of condition (c) uses only these two conditions, so the coefficients
vanish unless the edges form a matching. Thus
\[
c=\sum_M a_M\gamma_M,
\]
where $M$ runs over the $m$-matchings, oriented from $A$ to $B$ and ordered
by their $A$-endpoints. Indeed, expansion of $\gamma_M$ gives precisely
the signs under reversal just obtained.
Write $F$ for these coefficients on ordered oriented matchings, with
the usual signs under permutation and reversal.

There are also no terms of $z_g$ with a resting vertex in $B$.
For an $(m-1)$-matching $M'$ and a free vertex $b\in B$, the coefficient
with resting vertex $b$ therefore says
$F(ab,M')+F(a'b,M')=0$, where $a,a'$ are the two free vertices of $A$.
These are relations (R1) in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:top}.
Steps~1 and~2 of that proof use only (R1), and show that
$a_M=(-1)^{p(\alpha_M)}h(\beta_M)$ for a function $h$ on the free
$(r-1)$-subsets of $B$. Consequently $c=c_h$. Proposition~\ref{prop:universal}
now gives $z_g=\partial c_h=z_{U_{r-1}h}$, and injectivity of $g\mapsto z_g$
as a map of chains gives $g=U_{r-1}h$. This proves injectivity of $\Phi$.

Its image is generated by $\Phi(\delta_T)=x_{B\setminus T}$, $T\in\binom Br$,
and the column of $U_{r-1}$ indexed by $S\in\binom B{r-1}$, namely
$U_{r-1}\delta_S=\sum_{b\notin S}\delta_{S\cup b}$, gives exactly the displayed
relation for $C=B\setminus S$. Finally,
Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} identifies the torsion groups of the source
and target as abstract finite groups. The injection on torsion is
therefore surjective, proving the remaining assertion.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:pairing}
Let $r\ge1$, $N=m+r-1$, $T_0\in\binom{[N]}{r}$, and let $1\le n\le m$.  If
$k\,\delta_{T_0}\in\operatorname{im}U_{r-1}(N)$, then $n\mid k$.  Hence the class of
$\delta_{T_0}$ in $\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)$, if it has finite order, has order divisible by
$\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,m)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Put $B'_0=[N]\setminus T_0$, an $(m-1)$-set, and choose $Y\subset B'_0$ with
$|Y|=m-n$.  Let $y$ be the indicator function of the $(m-1)$-subsets containing
$Y$, and define the linear functional
$\lambda(g)=\sum_{T}g(T)\,y([N]\setminus T)$ on $\mathbb{Z}^{\binom{[N]}{r}}$.  For an
$(r-1)$-set $S$, the $m$-set $S^c=[N]\setminus S$ satisfies
\[
\lambda(U_{r-1}\delta_S)=\sum_{T\supset S}y(T^c)=\sum_{b\in S^c}y(S^c\setminus b)
=\#\{b\in S^c\setminus Y\}\cdot[\,Y\subset S^c\,]=n\,[\,Y\subset S^c\,]\equiv0\pmod n .
\]
So $\lambda$ vanishes modulo $n$ on $\operatorname{im}U_{r-1}$, while
$\lambda(\delta_{T_0})=y(B'_0)=1$.  Hence $k\delta_{T_0}\in\operatorname{im}U_{r-1}$
forces $k\equiv0\pmod n$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:torsgen}
Let $m\ge2$, $r\ge m$, $N=m+r-1$ and $K=K_{m+1,m+r-1}$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item $\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)$ is finite, and $\Phi$ is an isomorphism
      \[
      \Phi\colon\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z}).
      \]
\item The restricted theta classes $x_{B'}=[z_m^{(0)}|_{B'}]$, $B'\in\binom B{m-1}$,
      generate $\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$, and the relations
      $\sum_{B'\subset T}x_{B'}=0$, $T\in\binom Bm$, generate all relations among
      them.
\item Every $x_{B'}$ has order exactly $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,m)$, the exponent
      of $\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Put $q=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,m)$.  Since $r\ge m$ we have $s=m$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors}, so $q$ is the exponent of $\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:primary}).  In the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors},
$U_{r-1}(N)$ is equivalent to a diagonal matrix with nonzero entries $d_i=m-i$,
$0\le i\le m-1$, of total multiplicity $\binom N{m-1}=\binom N{r}$, the number of
rows.  Hence $\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)\cong\bigoplus_i(\mathbb{Z}/d_i)^{\nu_i}$ is finite, killed by
$q$, and of the same order as $\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$ by \eqref{eq:torsformula}.

(1) By Theorem~\ref{thm:theta-injective}, $\Phi$ is injective and its
image contains the entire torsion subgroup. Since its source is finite,
its image is exactly that torsion subgroup.

(2) The classes $\Phi(\delta_T)=x_{B\setminus T}$ generate because the $\delta_T$
generate $\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)$, and by (1) the relations among them are generated by the
columns $U_{r-1}\delta_S=\sum_{b\notin S}\delta_{S\cup b}$ of $U_{r-1}$, which in the
complementary indexing $B'=B\setminus T$ read $\sum_{B'\subset T'}x_{B'}=0$ with
$T'=B\setminus S\in\binom Bm$; these are the relations of Lemma~\ref{lem:wT}.

(3) By (1), the order of $x_{B'}$ equals the order of $\delta_{B\setminus B'}$ in
$\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)$, which divides $q$ and is divisible by $q$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:pairing}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:lowr}
In this range the theta subgroup has free rank
\[
\binom N{r}-\binom N{r-1}>0,\qquad N=m+r-1,
\]
by Theorems~\ref{thm:theta-injective} and~\ref{thm:exacttors}.
Each $\delta_T$ has infinite order in $\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}(N)$: if it lay in
$\operatorname{im}U_{r-1}\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, then by the symmetry of $[N]$ so would
every $\delta_{T'}$, contradicting the rank. Hence every restricted
theta class $x_{B'}$ has infinite order. Together with
Proposition~\ref{prop:theta}, this shows that the theta class on
$K_{m+1,m-1}$ survives with infinite order throughout $0\le r\le m-1$;
at $r=m$ it becomes torsion of order $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,m)$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:loop}
Let $m\ge1$ and $K=K_{m+1,2m}$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item For every perfect matching $P$ of $B$, $h_P\in\ker U_m(2m)$; hence $L_P$ is a
      cycle and $[L_P]\ne0$.
\item The classes $[L_P]$, $P$ non-nesting, form a basis of
      $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{C_m}$.  In representation-theoretic terms,
      $\ker U_m(2m)$ is the integral Specht module $S^{(m,m)}$ of $\Sigma_{2m}$, the
      $h_P$ are its polytabloids, and the $h_P$ with $P$ non-nesting are its
      standard basis.
\item $X_P$ is a connected orientable $m$-dimensional pseudomanifold: every
      $(m-1)$-cube of $X_P$ lies in exactly two $m$-cubes of $X_P$.  The chain
      $L_P$ is $\iota$ of its fundamental class.
\item For $m=2$, $UD_2(K_{3,4})$ is a deformation retract of the configuration
      space, and $X_P$ is a closed orientable surface of genus $2$ in which the three
      pairs of points over the configurations $\{a_i,a_j\}$ are identified.
      It has $19$ vertices, $48$ edges and $24$ squares,
      so $\chi(X_P)=-5$; the vertex links are $4$-cycles at the $12$ configurations
      $\{a,b\}$, $6$-cycles at the $4$ configurations $\{b,b'\}$ with $b,b'$ in
      different pairs, and two disjoint $4$-cycles at the $3$ configurations
      $\{a,a'\}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
(1) Let $T\in\binom B{m+1}$.  If $T$ misses a pair of $P$, then by counting it
contains two pairs entirely, and every $m$-subset of $T$ contains a full pair, so
$(U_mh_P)(T)=0$.  Otherwise $T$ meets every pair and contains exactly one pair
$\{i_k,j_k\}$ entirely; the only $m$-subsets $F\subset T$ with $h_P(F)\ne0$ are
$T\setminus i_k$ and $T\setminus j_k$, whose values differ by the factor $-1$ from
the $k$-th pair.  So $(U_mh_P)(T)=0$.  Since $h_P\ne0$, $L_P=c_{h_P}\ne0$, and there
are no boundaries in the top degree.

(2) A tabloid of shape $(m,m)$ is determined by its first row $F\in\binom Bm$, so
$M^{(m,m)}=\mathbb{Z}^{\binom Bm}$, and the polytabloid of a tableau $t$ with columns
$\{i_k,j_k\}$, $e_t=\sum_{\sigma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\{\sigma t\}$, is
$h_P$ for the perfect matching $P$ formed by the columns of $t$; $t$ is standard
exactly when $P$ is non-nesting.  By James \cite[Theorem~8.4]{James}, the standard
polytabloids are linearly independent over every field.  Hence the lattice
$\mathcal{L}$ spanned by the $h_P$, $P$ non-nesting, has rank $C_m$ and its reduction
modulo every prime is injective, so $\mathcal{L}$ is a saturated sublattice of
$\mathbb{Z}^{\binom Bm}$.  By (1), $\mathcal{L}\subset\ker U_m(2m)$, which is saturated of the
same rank $C_m$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors}.  Hence $\mathcal{L}=\ker U_m(2m)$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:universal} transports the basis to $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$.

(3) An $(m-1)$-cube of $X_P$ is a face of an $m$-cube $\gamma_M$: either a particle
comes to rest at $b\in B$, with the remaining crossings $M'$ covering $m-1$
vertices of $A$ and one vertex from each of the other $m-1$ pairs, and then the
$m$-cubes of $X_P$ containing it are $M'\cup\{ab\}$ and $M'\cup\{a'b\}$ for the two
free $A$-vertices $a,a'$; or a particle rests at $a\in A$, the crossings $M'$ cover
$m-1$ pairs, one pair $\{i_k,j_k\}$ is untouched, and the $m$-cubes of $X_P$
containing the face are $M'\cup\{ai_k\}$ and $M'\cup\{aj_k\}$, in which the
resting particle crosses into the untouched pair.  In both cases exactly two.  The coefficients
$\pm1$ of $L_P$ are compatible orientations, because $L_P$ is a cycle.  $X_P$ is
connected: the second type of face lets one particle switch between the two
vertices of its pair, and the first type lets the free $A$-vertex trade places with
any occupied $A$-vertex, and these moves connect all pairs $(\alpha,\sigma)$.
Finally $\iota$ sends the fundamental class $\sum_M\pm\gamma_M$ of $X_P$ to $L_P$
by definition.

(4) Abrams' theorem \cite{Abrams} applies to $UD_2(K_{3,4})$, since every cycle of
$K_{3,4}$ has length at least $4>3$.  Let $P=\{\{b_1,b_2\},\{b_3,b_4\}\}$.  The
$0$-cells of $X_P$ are the $3$ configurations $\{a,a'\}$, the $12$ configurations
$\{a,b\}$ and the $4$ configurations $\{b,b'\}$ with $b\in\{b_1,b_2\}$,
$b'\in\{b_3,b_4\}$; the $1$-cells are the $12\cdot4=48$ pairs (edge $ab$, resting
vertex outside $ab$ and outside the pair of $b$); the $2$-cells are the $24$
matchings $\{ab,a'b'\}$ with $b,b'$ in different pairs.  The squares containing
$\{a,b\}$ are $\{ab'',a'b\}$ with $b''$ in the other pair and $a'\ne a$: four,
forming a $4$-cycle.  The squares containing $\{b,b'\}$ are the six ordered pairs
$(a,a')$ with $a\ne a'$. Their link edges join the direction in which
$b$ moves to $a$ to the direction in which $b'$ moves to $a'$; the link
is therefore $K_{3,3}$ minus a perfect matching, hence a $6$-cycle.
The squares containing
$\{a,a'\}$ are $\{ab,a'b'\}$ with $b$ and $b'$ in different pairs: eight, and two
squares share an edge at $\{a,a'\}$ only if the particle at $a$ crosses into the
same pair in both; so the link is the disjoint union of two $4$-cycles, one for
each assignment of the two pairs to $a$ and $a'$.  Separating the two sheets at
these three vertices gives a closed surface with $22$ vertices, $48$ edges and $24$
faces, connected by (3), orientable by (3), of Euler characteristic $-2$, hence
of genus $2$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:universal}
Proposition~\ref{prop:universal} organizes the matching chains and theta cycles of this section.  The
matching chains $c_h$, $h\colon\binom B{r-1}\to R$, span the top chains that are
candidates for cycles, and the chains $z_g$, $g\colon\binom B{r}\to R$, are the
signed sums of restricted theta classes.  The boundary map between them is the
inclusion matrix $U_{r-1}$:
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
h\in\ker U_{r-1} &\leadsto& \text{top cycles; loop basis when }r=m+1,\\
h\equiv1,\ r=q &\leadsto& \partial w_m=qz_m,\\
h=\delta_{B\setminus T} &\leadsto&
 \partial w_T=\sum_{b\in T}z_m^{(0)}|_{T\setminus b},\\
g=\delta_T &\leadsto& \text{individual restricted theta cycles},\\
r=0 &\leadsto& \text{primitive generalized theta classes}.
\end{array}
\]
In the two extreme cases the crossings join the two parts: for $r=0$
the resting particle lies in the larger part $A$, whereas for $r=m+1$
the free $B$-vertices lie in the part of size $2m$.  The classical loop class ($m=1$, $r=2$) and the classical star class
($m=2$, $r=0$) sit at the two ends of this picture, and the torsion classes of
Theorem~B are what happens in between, when $U_{r-1}$ is neither injective nor
surjective modulo $r$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{rep:prop:arbitrary}
For every field $\Bbbk$ there is a natural $\Sigma_a\times\Sigma_b$-equivariant
isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:allfields}
 H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\Bbbk)\cong
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk\Sigma_m}\bigl(\operatorname{sgn},D_m(a;\Bbbk)\otimes D_m(b;\Bbbk)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here $\Sigma_m$ acts diagonally on the tensor product. Equivalently, the right
side is
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:homdual}
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk\Sigma_m}\bigl(D_m(a;\Bbbk)^*\otimes\operatorname{sgn},D_m(b;\Bbbk)\bigr).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
An ordered $m$-matching is specified by two injections
$\mathbf x:[m]\hookrightarrow[a]$ and $\mathbf y:[m]\hookrightarrow[b]$,
with edges $(x_i,y_i)$ in slot order. Proposition~\ref{prop:Zcycles} identifies top homology with functions $F(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ that are
alternating under simultaneous slot permutations and satisfy the vertex
sum relations.

At a fixed first-part vertex, a vertex sum varies one coordinate of
$\mathbf y$, keeping all of $\mathbf x$ and the other coordinates of
$\mathbf y$ fixed. Thus these relations give
$I_m(a;\Bbbk)\otimes D_m(b;\Bbbk)$. The second-part relations similarly give
$D_m(a;\Bbbk)\otimes I_m(b;\Bbbk)$; reversing the new edge contributes a common
minus sign and does not change the zero-sum equation. The intersection
of these two subspaces is $D_m(a;\Bbbk)\otimes D_m(b;\Bbbk)$, as one sees by choosing
vector-space complements to the two $D_m$'s. Finally, alternating slot
permutations pick out precisely the sign-equivariant vectors, giving
\eqref{rep:eq:allfields}.

For finite-dimensional representations, tensor--Hom adjunction gives
\eqref{rep:eq:homdual}. Neither step uses averaging by $1/m!$, semisimplicity,
or exactness of the invariants functor. The proof therefore applies also
when $\operatorname{char}\Bbbk$ divides $m!$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{rep:thm:rational}
For $m\ge1$ and $a,b\ge m$, there is a multiplicity-free decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:main}
 H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Q})\cong
 \bigoplus_{\substack{\lambda\vdash m\\
 \lambda_1\le a-m,\ \lambda'_1\le b-m}}
 S^{(a-m,\lambda)}\boxtimes S^{(b-m,\lambda')}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Insert \eqref{rep:eq:Ddecomp} for both factors in \eqref{rep:eq:allfields}.
The slot-group contribution from a pair $(\lambda,\mu)$ is
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}\Sigma_m}(\operatorname{sgn},S^\lambda\otimes S^\mu).
\]
Rational Specht modules are absolutely irreducible and self-dual, and
$S^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong S^{\lambda'}$. Schur's lemma therefore says
that the displayed space has dimension one if $\mu=\lambda'$ and is
zero otherwise. This gives \eqref{rep:eq:main}. Distinct $\lambda$ give
distinct first-factor shapes, so there are no repeated summands.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{rep:cor:rank}
Let $f^\rho$ be the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\rho$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:rank}
 \operatorname{rank} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})=
 \sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash m\\
 \lambda_1\le a-m,\ \lambda'_1\le b-m}}
 f^{(a-m,\lambda)}f^{(b-m,\lambda')}.
\end{equation}
Each factor is evaluated by the hook-length formula
\[
 f^\rho=\frac{|\rho|!}{\prod_{x\in\rho}h(x)}.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:nonzero}
 H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Q})\ne0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (a-m)(b-m)\ge m.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The weight-$m$ graph configuration chain complex is free abelian and has
no chains above degree $m$. Its top homology is therefore free abelian.
Its rank equals its rational dimension, yielding \eqref{rep:eq:rank}.
The allowable diagrams are exactly the partitions of $m$ contained in
a rectangle with $a-m$ columns and $b-m$ rows. Such a diagram exists
exactly when the rectangle has at least $m$ boxes.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The irreducible summands are indexed by partitions, not by individual
tableaux. After choosing standard Specht bases, their basis vectors are
indexed by pairs of standard Young tableaux of the indicated shapes.
Formula \eqref{rep:eq:rank} determines the integral top homology as an abstract
abelian group, but a rational decomposition alone does not determine its
integral equivariant lattice or give an integral direct-sum decomposition.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
For $a=m+1$, the only possible partition is $\lambda=(1^m)$.
Thus for $b\ge2m$ the rational top homology is
$\operatorname{sgn}_{\Sigma_{m+1}}\boxtimes S^{(b-m,m)}$.
At $b=2m$ this recovers the Specht module $S^{(m,m)}$ and its Catalan
rank, together with the sign action on the first part; see
Section~\ref{sec:loopclasses} for the integral polytabloid construction.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:rep-k55}
For $(m,a,b)=(3,5,5)$, the only allowed partition is $(2,1)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:25Q}
 H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{5,5};\mathbb{Q})
 \cong S^{(2,2,1)}\boxtimes S^{(2,2,1)},
 \qquad \dim_\mathbb{Q} H_3=5\cdot5=25.
\end{equation}
Indeed $f^{(2,2,1)}=5!/(4\cdot2\cdot3\cdot1\cdot1)=5$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:rep-polynomial}
For fixed $m$, there is a polynomial $P_m(a,b)\in\mathbb{Q}[a,b]$ of degree $m$
in each variable such that
\[
\operatorname{rank} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})=P_m(a,b)\qquad(a,b\ge2m).
\]
Its term of total degree $2m$ is $a^mb^m/m!$.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
In this range every partition of $m$ occurs in \eqref{rep:eq:rank}.
For fixed $\lambda\vdash m$, the hook-length formula makes
$f^{(a-m,\lambda)}$ a polynomial in $a$ of degree $m$, with leading
coefficient $f^\lambda/m!$. Since $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ and
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash m}(f^\lambda)^2=m!$, summing the products gives
both assertions.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{rep:lem:correction}
If $p\ge m$ is odd, then
\begin{align}
 &\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{F}_p)
 -\dim_\mathbb{Q} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Q})\notag\\
 &\hspace{2em}=\sum_{i=0}^{2m-2}(-1)^i
 \dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_i(G;\mathbb{F}_p^{\varepsilon}).\label{rep:eq:correction}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
For a field $\Bbbk$ let $A_i(\Bbbk)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk G}(\varepsilon,C_i(X;\Bbbk))$, with the
induced chain differential, and omit the augmentation from this complex.
Its top kernel is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk G}(\varepsilon,K_{\Bbbk})$ by left exactness, so its
top homology has the dimension in \eqref{rep:eq:joinidentity}.

For a projective $\Bbbk G$-module $M$, the norm map
\[
 (\varepsilon\otimes M)_G\longrightarrow(\varepsilon\otimes M)^G,
 \qquad [v]\longmapsto\sum_{g\in G}gv,
\]
is an isomorphism, natural in $M$. This is checked for the regular module
and hence for its direct summands; it does not require division by $|G|$.
Since $(\varepsilon\otimes M)^G\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk G}(\varepsilon,M)$,
these maps identify the complex $A_\bullet(\Bbbk)$ with the sign-twisted
coinvariant complex of $P_\bullet$ when $\Bbbk=\mathbb{F}_p$.
By \eqref{rep:eq:joinresolution}, its homology in degrees $0\le i<n$ is
$H_i(G;\Bbbk^{\varepsilon})$, while in the top degree the truncated complex has
kernel given by \eqref{rep:eq:joinidentity}.

Set $c_i=\dim_{\Bbbk} A_i(\Bbbk)$. These numbers are the same over $\mathbb{Q}$ and
over every field of odd characteristic. In fact, Frobenius reciprocity
shows that each simplex orbit contributes one if the sign character is
trivial on its stabilizer, and zero otherwise. Here the stabilizer is
$\Sigma_t$, and the contribution is one exactly when $t\le1$.
Euler characteristic, using that $n=2m-1$ is odd, now gives
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^ic_i
 =\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(-1)^i\dim_{\Bbbk} H_i(G;\Bbbk^{\varepsilon})
 -\dim_{\Bbbk} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\Bbbk)
\]
for $\Bbbk=\mathbb{F}_p$.
Over $\mathbb{Q}$, exactness of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q} G}(\varepsilon,-)$ and
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q} G}(\varepsilon,\mathbb{Q})=0$ show that $A_\bullet(\mathbb{Q})$ has homology
only at its top. Thus its Euler characteristic is
$-\dim_\mathbb{Q} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Q})$. Subtraction proves the formula.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{rep:lem:signhomology}
For an odd prime $p$ and $i\ge0$,
\[
 \dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_i(\Sigma_p;\mathbb{F}_p^{\operatorname{sgn}})=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&i\equiv p-2\text{ or }p-1\pmod{2(p-1)},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We recall the normalizer computation underlying this standard formula;
we use the stable-elements method for group cohomology
\cite[Chapter~XII]{CE}; see also \cite[Chapter~VI]{AM} and Swan's work
on groups with cyclic Sylow $p$-subgroups \cite{Swan}.
Let $C_p\le\Sigma_p$ be generated by a $p$-cycle. Its normalizer is
$C_p\rtimes\mathbb{F}_p^\times$. Distinct subgroups of order $p$ have trivial
intersection, so the stable-elements description identifies positive-degree
cohomology with coefficients in sign with the normalizer-invariant part
of $H^*(C_p;\mathbb{F}_p)\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$.

Write $H^*(C_p;\mathbb{F}_p)=\Lambda(u)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p[v]$, with $|u|=1$ and
$|v|=2$. A multiplier $c\in\mathbb{F}_p^\times$ acts on each of $u,v$ by $c$
(or by $c^{-1}$ under the opposite action convention), and its sign
as a permutation of $\mathbb{F}_p$ is $c^{(p-1)/2}$. Thus the invariant monomials
have degrees $p-2$ and $p-1$ modulo $2(p-1)$, one in each such degree.
Degree-zero cohomology is zero because sign is nontrivial.
Finally, over a field the dual of group homology with coefficients in
a finite-dimensional module is cohomology with coefficients in its dual;
sign is self-dual. This gives the stated homology dimensions.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{rep:thm:generalvanishing}
Let $m\ge2$, $a,b\ge2m-1$, and let $p\ge m$ be an odd prime. Then
\[
 \dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{F}_p)
 =\dim_\mathbb{Q} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Q}),
 \qquad H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})[p]=0.
\]
In particular the latter integral group has no $p$-primary torsion.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
If $p>m$, positive-degree group homology of $\Sigma_m$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$
vanishes by semisimplicity. Degree zero with sign coefficients also
vanishes because $m\ge2$ and $p$ is odd. Thus the correction in
\eqref{rep:eq:correction} is zero.

If $p=m$, Lemma~\ref{rep:lem:signhomology} shows that the only nonzero
terms in the range $0\le i\le2p-2$ occur in degrees $p-2$ and $p-1$.
Both have dimension one and their signs in the Euler sum are opposite.
The correction is again zero.

The integral top homology is free. Hence the universal coefficient
sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})\otimes\mathbb{F}_p
 \longrightarrow H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{F}_p)
 \longrightarrow H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})[p]
 \longrightarrow0
\]
and equality of dimensions prove the torsion assertion.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{rep:lem:two-local-slot}
For $n\ge5$, there is an isomorphism of $RG$-modules
\[
 D_n\cong\varepsilon^{\oplus(n-1)}\oplus P^{\oplus u_n}
          \oplus V^{\oplus v_n}.
\]
This assertion concerns the slot group only. In particular, the summands
$P$ are retained as integral modules, not split into trivial and sign
summands as they would be over $\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
For $c=(123)$ the element $e=(1+c+c^2)/3$ is a central idempotent of
$RG$, and $eRG\cong A:=R[C_2]$. Put
$T=\widetilde H_2(\Delta_{3,n};R)$, so that
$D_n\cong T\otimes\varepsilon$ by \eqref{rep:eq:chessboard}.
The chessboard complex has $3n$ vertices, $3n(n-1)$ edges, and
$n(n-1)(n-2)$ triangles. The slot group acts freely on the edges and
triangles; each of the $n$ vertex orbits is the three-point permutation
module. Applying $e$ to the augmented chain sequence therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{rep:eq:two-local-chess}
 0\longrightarrow eT\longrightarrow A^{\binom n3}
 \longrightarrow A^{\binom n2}\longrightarrow R^n
 \longrightarrow R\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Exactness follows from the concentration of reduced chessboard homology
in degree two. The action on $R^n$ is trivial and its augmentation is
summation, with kernel $R^{n-1}$.

Here $A$ is local, with maximal ideal $(2,t-1)$ for the generator $t$ of
$C_2$. An epimorphism $A^N\to R^d$ can be put, by a change of basis,
in the form of $d$ coordinate augmentations followed by zero coordinates;
its kernel is $\varepsilon^{\oplus d}\oplus A^{N-d}$.
The same assertion after twisting by sign gives kernel
$R^d\oplus A^{N-d}$ for an epimorphism $A^N\to\varepsilon^{\oplus d}$.
Apply the first assertion to the map onto $R^{n-1}$ in
\eqref{rep:eq:two-local-chess}. Split off the resulting free $A$-summand
from the preceding epimorphism; its complementary source is free since
$A$ is local. Applying the sign-twisted assertion to the remaining map
then gives
\[
 eT\cong R^{n-1}\oplus A^{\binom n3-\binom n2}.
\]
Since $A\otimes\varepsilon\cong A$, this proves
$eD_n\cong\varepsilon^{\oplus(n-1)}\oplus P^{\oplus u_n}$.

The action on $V$ identifies $(1-e)RG$ with $M_2(R)$. Indeed, in the
basis $(1,-1,0),(0,1,-1)$, the matrices of $c$ and $t=(12)$ are
\[
 c=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 t=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The four matrices $I,c,t,ct$ have coordinate determinant $\pm3$, a unit
of $R$, so the action map is surjective. Both algebras are free of rank
four, hence the map is an isomorphism. Matrix units consequently identify
every $R$-free module in this block with a sum of copies of $V$.
The rank of $T$ is $n^3-6n^2+8n-1$, by its Euler characteristic.
Subtracting the rank $(n-1)+2u_n$ of $eD_n$ leaves $2v_n$, proving
$(1-e)D_n\cong V^{\oplus v_n}$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{rep:prop:two-primary-three}
For $a,b\ge5$ and $S=\mathbb{Z}/2^\ell$, $\ell\ge1$,
\[
 H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{a,b};S)
 \cong S^{\beta_3(a,b)}\oplus S[2]^{(a-1)(b-1)},
 \qquad S[2]=\{x\in S:2x=0\},
\]
where $\beta_3(a,b)=\operatorname{rank} H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})$ is given by
\eqref{rep:eq:rank}. Explicitly,
\[
 \beta_3(a,b)=(a-1)u_b+(b-1)u_a+2u_au_b+v_av_b.
\]
Consequently the full torsion subgroup is
\[
 \operatorname{Tors} H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(a-1)(b-1)}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
For $n\ge5$, the augmented simplicial chain sequence of $\Delta_{3,n}$,
with its top kernel included, is split exact as a sequence of abelian
groups: the reduced integral homology is free and concentrated in degree
two. Thus formation of the top kernel commutes with base change, and
its inclusion in the top chain module is split over the coefficient ring.
Using \eqref{rep:eq:chessboard}, the tensor-intersection argument of
Proposition~\ref{rep:prop:arbitrary} therefore applies over $S$, giving
\[
 H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{a,b};S)
 \cong\operatorname{Hom}_{SG}
 (\varepsilon_S,D_{a,S}\otimes_S D_{b,S}),
 \qquad D_{n,S}=D_n\otimes_R S.
\]

Apply Lemma~\ref{rep:lem:two-local-slot}. For the summands in the
$C_3$-trivial block, we have
\[
 \varepsilon_S\otimes\varepsilon_S\cong S,\qquad
 \varepsilon_S\otimes P_S\cong P_S,\qquad
 P_S\otimes P_S\cong P_S^{\oplus2}.
\]
The sign-equivariant vectors in $S$ form $S[2]$, whereas those in $P_S$
form a free copy of $S$, generated by the difference of its two basis
vectors. Tensor products of $V_S$ with either $\varepsilon_S$ or $P_S$
have no sign-equivariant vectors, since their $C_3$-invariant part is zero.
Finally, the perfect wedge pairing and $\det V_S=\varepsilon_S$ give
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_{SG}(\varepsilon_S,V_S\otimes_S V_S)
 \cong\operatorname{End}_{SG}(V_S)\cong S;
\]
the last equality follows because the action spans $M_2(S)$.
Thus the only nonfree contribution is $S[2]^{(a-1)(b-1)}$, and the
free contributions have the asserted total rank $\beta_3(a,b)$.
The same calculation over $\mathbb{Q}$ identifies this rank with
\eqref{rep:eq:rank}.

The integral top homology is free of rank $\beta_3(a,b)$. The split
universal coefficient sequence and cancellation of the common finite
summand $S^{\beta_3(a,b)}$ give
\[
 \operatorname{Tor}\bigl(H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{a,b};\mathbb{Z}),S\bigr)
 \cong S[2]^{(a-1)(b-1)}\qquad(\ell\ge1).
\]
Taking $\ell=1$ counts the $2$-primary cyclic factors, and $\ell=2$
excludes factors of order $4$ or higher. Every odd prime satisfies
$p\ge3$, so Theorem~\ref{rep:thm:generalvanishing} excludes all odd
 torsion, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:external-products}
Following \cite[Definition~5.10]{ADK} and \cite[Section~3.1]{AK},
for disjoint subgraphs $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2\subset\Gamma$ we call the map
\[
 H_i(\mathbb{B}_{n_1}\Gamma_1;\mathbb{Z})\otimes H_j(\mathbb{B}_{n_2}\Gamma_2;\mathbb{Z})
 \longrightarrow H_{i+j}(\mathbb{B}_{n_1+n_2}\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})
\]
obtained by the homology cross product followed by the union map
$(\xi_1,\xi_2)\mapsto\xi_1\cup\xi_2$ the \emph{external product}.
We denote its value by $\alpha\times\beta$; in particular,
$[C]\times\sigma$ denotes the product of a loop class and a star class
supported in disjoint subgraphs. The construction depends on the chosen
disjoint supports.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:loop-star-torsion}
Let $\Gamma=K_{a,b}$ with $a,b\ge5$, and enumerate its parts as
$A=\{a_0,\ldots,a_{a-1}\}$ and $B=\{b_0,\ldots,b_{b-1}\}$.
For $1\le i<a$ and $1\le j<b$, let
\[
 C_{ij}=a_0b_0a_ib_ja_0
\]
be the indicated $4$-cycle, and let $\Lambda_{ij}\cong K_{a-2,b-2}$ be
the induced subgraph on the vertices outside $C_{ij}$. Choose a star
class $\sigma_{ij}\in H_1(\mathbb{B}_2\Lambda_{ij};\mathbb{Z})$. Then
\[
 t_{ij}=[C_{ij}]\times\sigma_{ij}
 \in H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})
\]
form an $\mathbb{F}_2$-basis of $\operatorname{Tors} H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$.
In particular, every torsion class is a sum of loop--star products.
There is a canonical isomorphism
\[
 \Theta\colon\operatorname{Tors} H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})
 \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb{F}_2)
\]
sending $t_{ij}$ to $[C_{ij}]$ modulo $2$.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The cycles $C_{ij}$ form an integral basis of $H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$: they
are the fundamental cycles for the spanning tree consisting of all
edges incident to $a_0$ or $b_0$. Each $\Lambda_{ij}$ is $3$-connected
and non-planar, so its star classes have order $2$
\cite[Lemmas~C.4 and~C.9]{ADK}. Since $C_{ij}$ and $\Lambda_{ij}$ are
disjoint, the union map above is defined and $2t_{ij}=0$.
It remains to prove that these products are independent.

For a loop in $\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma$, summing the trajectories of its three
particles gives an integral $1$-cycle in $\Gamma$, even when the
particles are permuted. This construction is invariant under homotopy
and additive under concatenation, and defines the total trace
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\colon H_1(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb{Z}).
\]
Let $\eta\in H^1(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma;\mathbb{F}_2)$ be the character recording the
parity of the permutation of the three particles, obtained from the
ordered configuration covering. For $\alpha\in H^1(\Gamma;\mathbb{F}_2)$,
write $\operatorname{tr}^*\alpha$ for the degree-one cohomology class
obtained by composition with total trace.

Represent $t_{ij}$ by a torus whose first circle moves one particle
around $C_{ij}$ and whose second circle exchanges two particles in
the chosen star. Along the first circle, total trace is $[C_{ij}]$
and permutation parity is zero. Along the second, total trace is zero,
because the trajectories lie in a tree, and permutation parity is one.
Consequently, writing $\rho_2$ for reduction of homology modulo $2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loop-star-pairing}
 \bigl\langle\operatorname{tr}^*\alpha\smile\eta,\rho_2(t_{ij})\bigr\rangle
 =\langle\alpha,[C_{ij}]\rangle.
\end{equation}
Taking the cohomology basis dual to the $C_{ij}$ proves that the
$(a-1)(b-1)$ products are nonzero and independent. They therefore form
a basis of the torsion subgroup by Proposition~\ref{rep:prop:two-primary-three}.

For a torsion class $t$, define $\Theta(t)$ by the identities
\[
 \langle\alpha,\Theta(t)\rangle
 =\bigl\langle\operatorname{tr}^*\alpha\smile\eta,\rho_2(t)\bigr\rangle
 \quad\text{for all }\alpha\in H^1(\Gamma;\mathbb{F}_2).
\]
The perfect pairing over $\mathbb{F}_2$ makes this definition unique.
Equation~\eqref{eq:loop-star-pairing} shows that $\Theta$ sends the
displayed basis to the cycle basis, hence is an isomorphism. Its
definition uses no choices of a spanning tree or star representatives.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{rep:cor:allprimecounterexample}
For each odd prime $p$, the inclusion
\[
 K_{p+1,\,2p-1}\hookrightarrow K_{2p-1,\,2p-1}
\]
is a counterexample to upward persistence of the existence of $p$-torsion
in degree $p-1$ with $p$ particles. More precisely, the source homology
has a $\mathbb{Z}/p$ direct summand, whereas
\[
 H_{p-1}(\mathbb{B}_pK_{2p-1,\,2p-1};\mathbb{Z})[p]=0.
\]
The induced map annihilates the entire $p$-primary torsion of the source.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
