Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} with
$m=p$ and $r=p$. Its $j=p$ summand is $\mathbb{Z}/p$, with multiplicity
$\binom{2p-1}{0}-\binom{2p-1}{-1}=1$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{rep:thm:generalvanishing} to the target with $m=p$ and
$a=b=2p-1$. A homomorphism sends a $p$-power-torsion element to a
$p$-power-torsion element, so the final assertion follows as well.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:second-part-persistence}
Let $q\ge2$, $m\ge q$, and $r\ge q$. Under the inclusion
\[
\iota_r\colon K_{m+1,m+q-1}\hookrightarrow K_{m+1,m+r-1}
\]
obtained by adding vertices to the second part, the image of
$[z_m^{(q)}]$ has order exactly $q$.
If $m=q=p$ is prime, the induced map on $p$-primary torsion is an
isomorphism; both groups are $\mathbb{Z}/p$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Let $B_0\subseteq B$ be the second part of the source, so
$|B_0|=m+q-1$ and $|B|=m+r-1$. Use the same ordering of $A$ in both graphs.
The inclusion of chain complexes sends each restricted theta cycle
$z_m^{(0)}|_{B'}$ of the source to the restricted theta cycle of the
target with the same $B'$. By \eqref{eq:zsum}, the image of the source class is
\[
\Phi([g]),\qquad
g=\sum_{B'\in\binom{B_0}{m-1}}\delta_{B\setminus B'}.
\]
It is killed by $q$, since the source class has order $q$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:explicitgen}. We prove that its order is divisible
by every maximal prime power $d=p^a$ dividing $q$.

Choose $Y\subset B_0$ with $|Y|=m-d$, and define
\[
\lambda_Y(f)=\sum_{\substack{T\in\binom B{r}\\Y\subseteq B\setminus T}}f(T).
\]
For $S\in\binom B{r-1}$, the calculation in Lemma~\ref{lem:pairing} gives
\[
\lambda_Y(U_{r-1}\delta_S)=d\,[\,Y\subseteq B\setminus S\,].
\]
Thus $\lambda_Y$ descends to a homomorphism
$\operatorname{coker} U_{r-1}\to\mathbb{Z}/d$. On the indicated element it takes the value
\[
\lambda_Y(g)=\binom{|B_0|-|Y|}{m-1-|Y|}
=\binom{q+d-1}{d-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
For the congruence, $d=p^a$ divides $q$, so the lowest $a$ base-$p$
digits of $q+d-1$ and $d-1$ are all $p-1$, while all higher digits
of $d-1$ are zero; Lucas' theorem applies. This value is a unit
modulo $d$, and therefore $[g]$ has order divisible by $d$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:theta-injective} preserves this order under $\Phi$.
Doing this for each prime divisor of $q$ proves that the image has
order exactly $q$.

When $m=q=p$, Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} gives exactly one
$p$-primary cyclic factor, of order $p$, in both source and target.
The nonzero induced map is consequently an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:pendant}
There is a chain homotopy equivalence over the ring $\mathbb{Z}[E(\Gamma)]$
\[
\widetilde{S}(\Gamma')\;\simeq\;\widetilde{S}(\Gamma)\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{j\ge1}\widetilde{S}(\Gamma_v)[1,j+1]^{\oplus(d-1)}.
\]
Consequently, for every $i,n\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pendantsplit}
H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma')\cong H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)\oplus\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n-2}H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_v)^{\oplus(d-1)}.
\end{equation}
The inclusion $\Gamma\hookrightarrow\Gamma'$ realizes the first direct summand.  These
statements remain valid with coefficients in any commutative ring.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Put $T=\widetilde{S}(\Gamma_v)$, $S=\widetilde{S}(\Gamma)$, and retain the special half-edge $h_v$ at $v$.
For every other old half-edge $h$ at $v$, write $\xi_h=h-h_v$ and $a_h=e(h)-e(h_v)$, so
that $\partial\xi_h=a_h$.  Take $g=h_\ell-h_v$ and $u=\ell-e(h_v)$.  Then $\partial g=u$
and
\[
\widetilde{S}(\Gamma')=S[u]\oplus g\,T[u],\qquad\partial(gy)=u\,\iota(y)-g\,\partial y.
\]
Give $u^aX$ auxiliary degree $a$ and $u^agY$ auxiliary degree $a+1$.  The differential
preserves this degree; degree zero is precisely $S$.  For each $j\ge1$ the remaining
piece is
\[
C_j=u^jT\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{h\ne h_v}u^j\xi_hT\ \oplus\ u^{j-1}gT .
\]
Make the triangular change of generators
\[
z_{h,j}=u^j\xi_h-a_h\,u^{j-1}g .
\]
This is an invertible graded $\mathbb{Z}[E]$-linear change of basis.  The generator $z_{h,j}$ has
bidegree $(1,j+1)$ and satisfies $\partial z_{h,j}=0$, so $z_{h,j}T\cong T[1,j+1]$ as
chain complexes.  The remaining subcomplex $u^jT\oplus u^{j-1}gT$ is a shifted cone of
the identity on $T$, hence contractible.  Explicitly, a contraction sends $u^jy$ to
$u^{j-1}gy$ and sends $u^{j-1}gy$ to zero.  Thus
\[
C_j\cong\operatorname{cone}(\mathrm{id}_T)[0,j]\oplus T[1,j+1]^{\oplus(d-1)} .
\]
Discarding the contractible pieces proves the chain homotopy equivalence.  In total
weight $n$ the second summand has weight $k=n-j-1$ in $T$, which gives
\eqref{eq:pendantsplit}.  The construction also identifies the original complex with the
degree-zero summand, and works over every coefficient ring without a flatness assumption.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:pendantall}
For every prime $p$,
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_pH_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_pH_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)\oplus\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n-2}\operatorname{Tors}_pH_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_v)^{\oplus(d-1)}.
\]
Thus pendant attachment never kills torsion.  For $d\ge2$ it preserves the entire
$p$-primary subgroup in degree $i$, weight $n$, if and only if $H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_v)$ has
no $p$-torsion for $0\le k\le n-2$.  For $d=1$ it preserves the whole homology in every
degree and weight.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Take the torsion subgroups in \eqref{eq:pendantsplit}.  The criterion follows since all
these torsion groups are finite.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:pendant}
Attaching a pendant edge at a nonisolated vertex preserves odd torsion in $H_2$: for
every odd prime $p$ and every $n$,
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma).
\]
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Every extra torsion summand in Corollary~\ref{cor:pendantall} is $p$-torsion in an
$H_1(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_v)$, which is zero for odd $p$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}.  Repeating the
argument treats any finite sequence of such attachments.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:topminusone}
Let $m\ge2$.  Attaching a pendant edge at any vertex of a finite graph preserves the
full torsion subgroup of $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$, including the $2$-primary part.  At a
nonisolated vertex the stronger formula is
\[
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma')\cong H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma)\oplus H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-2}\Gamma_v)^{\oplus(d-1)},
\]
and the added summand is free abelian.  Moreover, if $J$ is a disjoint union of arcs and
points, then
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m(\Gamma\sqcup J))\cong\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma).
\]
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
In \eqref{eq:pendantsplit}, with $i=m-1$ and $n=m$, the groups at $k<m-2$ vanish, and
the group at $k=m-2$ is top homology, hence free by Observation~\ref{obs:top}.

Every component of every configuration space of $J$ is contractible.  The K\"unneth
decomposition therefore expresses $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m(\Gamma\sqcup J))$ as a sum of copies of
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_a\Gamma)$, with $a\le m$.  The term $a=m$ occurs once, the terms $a=m-1$ are
free top homology, and the terms $a<m-1$ vanish.  This proves the second assertion.  If
the attaching vertex is isolated, attaching the first edge replaces an isolated point
component by an arc component; the same argument shows that this also preserves the
indicated torsion subgroup.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{ex:pendantfail}
Let $\Delta$ be a graph, attach a path $x-v-w$ at $x\in\Delta$, and call the resulting
graph $\Gamma$.  Attach a new pendant edge at the bivalent vertex $v$, obtaining
$\Gamma'$.  Then $\Gamma_v\cong(\Delta\cup\text{pendant at }x)\sqcup I$, where $I$ is an
arc.  With $\Delta=K_{3,3}$, Corollary~\ref{cor:pendantall} and Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone}
give
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_2H_2(\mathbb{B}_4\Gamma')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_2H_2(\mathbb{B}_4\Gamma)\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2 .
\]
Only the extra term $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2\Gamma_v)$ has torsion, and its torsion is $\mathbb{Z}/2$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:r2} and Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone}. With $\Delta=K_{4,5}$ instead, the same splittings
give
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_3H_3(\mathbb{B}_5\Gamma')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_3H_3(\mathbb{B}_5\Gamma)\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3 .
\]
Here the only extra term with $3$-torsion is $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma_v)$, whose $3$-primary part
is $\mathbb{Z}/3$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:exact}.  Thus neither all-prime invariance in $H_2$ for
arbitrary particle number, nor odd-torsion invariance in arbitrary degree, follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:pendant}; both unrestricted assertions are false.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:loop}
There is an isomorphism of chain complexes
\[
\widetilde{S}(\Gamma'')\cong\widetilde{S}(\Gamma')\oplus c\cdot\widetilde{S}(\Gamma_v)[u],
\]
where $c$ has bidegree $(1,1)$ and $\partial(cy)=-c\,\partial y$.  Consequently, for all
$i$ and $n$,
\[
H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma'')\cong H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma')\oplus\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n-1}H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_v).
\]
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Let $h_1,h_2$ be the two half-edges of $e_0$ at $v$, and let $g_j=h_j-h_v$.  Then
$\partial g_1=\partial g_2=e_0-e(h_v)$, so $c=g_1-g_2$ is a cycle.  In the basis
$\{g_1,c\}$ of the new generators at $v$, write
\[
\widetilde{S}(\Gamma'')=A\oplus g_1B\oplus cB,\qquad A=\widetilde{S}(\Gamma)[u],\quad B=\widetilde{S}(\Gamma_v)[u],\quad u=e_0-e(h_v).
\]
The subcomplex $A\oplus g_1B$ is identified with $\widetilde{S}(\Gamma')$ by $e_0\mapsto\ell$ and
$g_1\mapsto h_\ell-h_v$; compare the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pendant}.  Since $\partial c=0$,
$\partial(cy)=-c\,\partial y$, so $cB$ is also a subcomplex.  Hence the sum is a direct sum of
complexes.

Finally, $H_i(cB)_n=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}u^jH_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1-j}\Gamma_v)$.  Geometrically, one
particle runs once around the loop, $j$ particles rest on it, and the remaining
$k=n-1-j$ particles move in $\Gamma_v$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{cor:loop}
For every $i,n\ge0$,
\[
H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma'')\cong H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)\oplus H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_v)\oplus\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n-2}H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_v)^{\oplus d}.
\]
The same direct-sum formula holds after taking $\operatorname{Tors}_p$, for every prime $p$.  In
particular, attaching a simple cycle at one nonisolated vertex preserves odd torsion in
$H_2$ for every particle number, but can create $2$-torsion there.  It never kills
existing torsion in any degree.  In degree $m-1$ with $m$ particles, the torsion formula
simplifies to
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_pH_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma'')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_pH_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma)\oplus\operatorname{Tors}_pH_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_v).
\]
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Combine Proposition~\ref{prop:loop} with \eqref{eq:pendantsplit}.  For $i=2$, the extra
$H_1$ groups have only $2$-torsion by Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}.  For $i=m-1$ and $n=m$, the
terms with $k\le m-2$ are free or zero by Observation~\ref{obs:top}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:alldegrees}
Let $L_0=K_{4,5}$, and let $L_{j+1}$ be $L_j$ with a lollipop attached at a vertex of
$L_j$.  Then $H_{2+j}(\mathbb{B}_{3+j}L_j;\mathbb{Z})$ contains an element of order $3$ for every
$j\ge0$.  Hence $3$-torsion occurs in every degree $\ge2$.
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Let $\Gamma=L_j\cup(\text{edge }xv)$, so that $L_{j+1}=\Gamma\cup(\text{loop at }v)$ and
$\Gamma_v\cong L_j\cup(\text{pendant at }x)$.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:loop} with $k=n-1$,
\[
H_{3+j}(\mathbb{B}_{4+j}L_{j+1})\supseteq H_{2+j}(\mathbb{B}_{3+j}(L_j\cup\text{pendant})).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:pendant}, $H_i(\mathbb{B}_nL_j)$ is a direct summand of
$H_i(\mathbb{B}_n(L_j\cup\text{pendant}))$, so an element of order $3$ survives.  The case $j=0$
is Theorem~\ref{thm:explicitgen}.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:parallel}
There is a decomposition of chain complexes $\widetilde{S}(\Gamma^+)=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}C_j$ with
\[
C_0=S,\qquad C_1=\operatorname{cone}\bigl(S_u\oplus S_w\to S\bigr)[0,1],\qquad
C_j\simeq\bigl(S/(S_u+S_w)\bigr)[0,j]\ \ (j\ge2),
\]
where $[0,j]$ shifts the weight by $j$ and $\simeq$ denotes a quasi-isomorphism.
Consequently, for all $i$ and $n$,
\[
H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)\cong H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)\ \oplus\ H_i(C_1)_n\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{k=0}^{n-4}H_{i-2}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_{uw})^{\oplus(d(u)-1)(d(w)-1)},
\]
and $C_1$ sits in a long exact sequence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\cdots&\longrightarrow H_i(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_u)\oplus H_i(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_w)
 \longrightarrow H_i(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma)\\
&\longrightarrow H_i(C_1)_n
 \longrightarrow H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_u)\oplus H_{i-1}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_w)
 \longrightarrow\cdots .
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
\emph{Choice of generators.}  Take the special half-edges $h_u$ and $h_w$ to be the two
half-edges of $e$.  The new half-edges $h'_u,h'_w$ of $e'$ give generators
$g_u=h'_u-h_u$ and $g_w=h'_w-h_w$ with
\[
\partial g_u=\partial g_w=e'-e=:t .
\]
Then $\mathbb{Z}[E][e']=\mathbb{Z}[E][t]$, and every cell of $\widetilde{S}(\Gamma^+)$ has a unique form
\[
t^aX,\qquad t^ag_uY,\qquad t^ag_wZ,\qquad t^ag_ug_wW,
\]
with $X\in S$, $Y\in S_u$, $Z\in S_w$ and $W\in S_u\cap S_w$.

\emph{The grading.}  Define the $t$-degree of a cell as $a$ plus the number of $g$'s.
The differential preserves it: $\partial g_u=\partial g_w=t$, and all other differentials
do not involve $t$.  Hence $\widetilde{S}(\Gamma^+)=\bigoplus_jC_j$, where $C_j$ is spanned by cells
of $t$-degree $j$.

\emph{Identifying the pieces.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item $C_0=S$.
\item $C_1=tS\oplus g_uS_u\oplus g_wS_w$, with
      $\partial(g_uY)=tY-g_u\partial Y$ and
      $\partial(g_wZ)=tZ-g_w\partial Z$, identifies with
      $\operatorname{cone}(f)[0,1]$, where
      $f\colon S_u\oplus S_w\to S$, $f(Y,Z)=Y+Z$, is the sum of the two
      inclusions.
\item For $j\ge2$, $C_j=t^jS\oplus t^{j-1}g_uS_u\oplus t^{j-1}g_wS_w\oplus t^{j-2}g_ug_w(S_u\cap S_w)$
      is the total complex of the commutative square of inclusions
      $S_u\cap S_w\to S_u,S_w\to S$.  Since these are inclusions of subcomplexes with
      $S_u\cap S_w$ as intersection, the total complex is quasi-isomorphic to
      $S/(S_u+S_w)$.
\end{itemize}

\emph{The quotient.}  The quotient $S/(S_u+S_w)$ is spanned by the cells in which both $u$
and $w$ carry generators.  The differential of those generators lands in $S_u+S_w$, so
\[
S/(S_u+S_w)\cong\bigoplus_{h\ne h_u,\ h'\ne h_w}\widetilde{S}(\Gamma_{uw})[2,2].
\]

\emph{Weights.}  In weight $n$, the piece $C_j$ involves $\widetilde{S}(\Gamma_{uw})$ in weight
$n-j-2$, so only $j\le n-2$, i.e.\ $k=n-j-2\ge0$, contributes.  The piece $C_1$ involves
$S$, $S_u$, $S_w$ in weight $n-1$.  This gives the stated formula and the long exact
sequence.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:parallel-top}
Let $\Gamma^+=\Gamma\cup e'$ be obtained by adding an edge parallel to
$e=uw$, with $u\ne w$.  For every $m\ge1$ and every commutative ring $R$,
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma^+;R)
\cong
H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;R)
\oplus
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_{uw};R).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma^+;\mathbb{Z})
\cong
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})
\oplus
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_{uw};\mathbb{Z}).
\]
The same statement holds primary-componentwise at every prime.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Use the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:parallel}.  In degree $m$ and weight $m$,
the terms $C_{j\ge2}$ do not contribute: their homology groups are of the form
\[
H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_{uw}),\qquad k\le m-4,
\]
and vanish because the homological degree exceeds the particle number.

The long exact sequence for $C_1$ therefore gives
\[
H_m(C_1)_m\cong
\ker\!\left(
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_u;R)\oplus
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_w;R)
\longrightarrow
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma;R)
\right),
\]
since $H_m(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}-;R)=0$.

Put $T=S_u\cap S_w$ and $U=S_u+S_w$.  In weight $m-1$, the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow S_u\oplus S_w\longrightarrow U\longrightarrow0
\]
shows that
\[
H_{m-1}(T)_{m-1}\longrightarrow
H_{m-1}(S_u\oplus S_w)_{m-1}
\]
is injective, because $H_m(U)_{m-1}=0$.  Moreover
\[
S/U\cong T[2,2]^{\oplus(d(u)-1)(d(w)-1)}
\]
and hence
\[
H_m(S/U)_{m-1}
\cong
H_{m-2}(T)_{m-3}^{\oplus(d(u)-1)(d(w)-1)}
=0.
\]
Thus $H_{m-1}(U)_{m-1}\to H_{m-1}(S)_{m-1}$ is injective, and the displayed kernel
is precisely
\[
H_{m-1}(T)_{m-1}\cong H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_{uw};R).
\]
Together with $C_0=S$, this proves the first formula.

For the torsion statement, apply the first formula with
$R=\mathbb{Z}/\ell^a$ for every prime $\ell$ and every $a\ge1$.  The integral top homology
groups
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_m-;\mathbb{Z}),\qquad H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}-;\mathbb{Z})
\]
are free.  Comparing the split universal coefficient sequences and cancelling the
common free tensor summands gives
\[
\operatorname{Tor}\!\left(H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma^+;\mathbb{Z}),R\right)
\cong
\operatorname{Tor}\!\left(H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z}),R\right)
\oplus
\operatorname{Tor}\!\left(H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}\Gamma_{uw};\mathbb{Z}),R\right).
\]
Comparison for all $\ell$ and $a$ determines the elementary divisors and gives the
claimed torsion splitting.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:parallel}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item $H_*(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ is a direct summand of $H_*(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)$.  Hence adding a parallel
      edge never kills torsion, and deleting one of several parallel edges never
      creates torsion.  This holds for every prime and every degree.
\item For every odd prime $p$,
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)\cong\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)\oplus\operatorname{Tors}_p\operatorname{coker}\Bigl(H_2(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_u)\oplus H_2(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_w)\to H_2(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma)\Bigr).
\]
\item Suppose $d(u),d(w)\ge2$.  Then, in degrees $i\ge3$, $\operatorname{Tors} H_{i-2}(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_{uw})$ is a
      direct summand of $\operatorname{Tors} H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)$ for each $k\le n-4$, with multiplicity
      $(d(u)-1)(d(w)-1)$.  In particular, if $H_2(\mathbb{B}_k\Gamma_{uw})$ has odd torsion for
      some $k\le n-4$, then adding $e'$ produces new odd torsion summands in
      $H_4(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Part (1) is immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:parallel}.  For (2): the summands coming
from $C_{j\ge2}$ contribute $H_0$'s to $H_2$, which are free.  In the long exact sequence
for $C_1$, the term following $H_2(C_1)$ is a subgroup of $H_1\oplus H_1$, which has no
odd torsion by Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}.  So after localizing at $p$ the sequence splits.
Part (3) is read off from Theorem~\ref{thm:parallel}.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:Dn}
With the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:parallel}, put
\[
T=S_u\cap S_w,\qquad U=S_u+S_w,\qquad
\mu=(d(u)-1)(d(w)-1).
\]
For $n\ge0$ define
\[
D_n=
\operatorname{coker}\!\left(
H_n(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma_u)\oplus H_n(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma_w)
\longrightarrow H_n(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)
\right).
\]
Then there is a short exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow E_n\longrightarrow D_n\longrightarrow L_n\longrightarrow0,
\]
where
\[
E_n=
\ker\!\left(
H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma_{uw})
\longrightarrow
H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma_u)\oplus H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma_w)
\right)
\]
and
\[
L_n\subseteq
H_{n-2}(\mathbb{B}_{n-2}\Gamma_{uw})^{\oplus\mu}.
\]
In particular $L_n$ is free abelian and
\[
\operatorname{Tors} D_n\cong\operatorname{Tors} E_n.
\]
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
The exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow T\xrightarrow{(1,-1)}
S_u\oplus S_w\longrightarrow U\longrightarrow0
\]
gives, in weight $n$,
\[
H_n(U)_n\big/
\operatorname{im}\!\left(
H_n(S_u)_n\oplus H_n(S_w)_n
\right)
\cong E_n.
\]
Indeed, this quotient is the image of the connecting map to
$H_{n-1}(T)_n$, hence the displayed kernel.

Next write
\[
Q=S/U\cong T[2,2]^{\oplus\mu}.
\]
Then
\[
H_{n+1}(Q)_n
\cong H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_{n-2}\Gamma_{uw})^{\oplus\mu}=0,
\]
because the homological degree exceeds the particle number.  Thus
$H_n(U)_n\to H_n(S)_n$ is injective.  Quotienting by the common image of
$H_n(S_u)_n\oplus H_n(S_w)_n$ gives
\[
0\longrightarrow E_n\longrightarrow D_n\longrightarrow L_n\longrightarrow0,
\]
where $L_n$ is the image of $D_n$ in
\[
H_n(Q)_n
\cong H_{n-2}(\mathbb{B}_{n-2}\Gamma_{uw})^{\oplus\mu}.
\]
The latter is top homology and hence free.  Therefore $L_n$ is free, the
short exact sequence splits as abelian groups, and
$\operatorname{Tors} D_n\cong\operatorname{Tors} E_n$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{cor:parallel3}
For every odd prime $p$ and every $0\le n\le3$,
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)\cong\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma).
\]
Thus adding or deleting parallel edges does not change odd torsion in $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma)$.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
For $n\le2$, both groups are zero by Observation~\ref{obs:top}.  For $n=3$,
Theorem~\ref{prop:parallel-top} identifies the extra torsion with that of
$H_1(\mathbb{B}_2\Gamma_{uw})$, which has no odd torsion by Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}.
Iteration proves the assertion
for any number of parallel edges.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:loopfail}
Attach an edge $xv$ at a vertex of a graph $\Delta$, where $v$ is new, and call this
graph $\Gamma$.  Add a loop at the univalent vertex $v$ to obtain $\Gamma''$.  Since
$\Gamma_v\cong\Gamma$, Theorem~\ref{cor:loop} and the top-minus-one pendant invariance
give
\begin{align*}
\Delta=K_{3,3}:&\quad \operatorname{Tors}_2H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma'')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_2H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma)\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\\
\Delta=K_{4,5}:&\quad \operatorname{Tors}_3H_3(\mathbb{B}_4\Gamma'')\cong\operatorname{Tors}_3H_3(\mathbb{B}_4\Gamma)\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3 .
\end{align*}
In each case only the highest-weight added term can have the indicated torsion.  The
same examples arise from parallel-edge attachment: start with $\Delta\cup(x-v-w)$ and
double the edge $vw$.  The graph before attachment is homeomorphic to $\Gamma$, and the
graph afterwards to $\Gamma''$.  Thus $2$-primary invariance in
Corollary~\ref{cor:parallel3}, and invariance of odd torsion in all homological degrees,
would both be false.  All three attachment operations nevertheless preserve existing
torsion as a direct summand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:pendant}, Theorem~\ref{cor:loop}, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:parallel}(1).
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:extend}
Let $\Gamma$ be a simple graph and $C\subseteq\Gamma$ a subgraph.  Extension by zero
defines an injective map
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;R)\hookrightarrow H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;R)
\]
for every $m\ge1$ and every commutative ring $R$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Use Proposition~\ref{prop:Zcycles}.  Let $F$ be a matching function on $C$ satisfying
\eqref{eq:Z} for $C$, and extend it by zero to the ordered oriented $m$-matchings of
$\Gamma$.  The extension is alternating and odd under reversal.  Consider \eqref{eq:Z}
for $\Gamma$ at $(M',v)$.  If $M'\not\subset C$ or $v\notin V(C)$, every term vanishes.
Otherwise the terms with $vx\notin E(C)$ vanish, and the remaining sum runs over
$x\in N_C(v)\setminus V(M')$, which is \eqref{eq:Z} for $C$.  So the extension is a top
cycle of $\Gamma$, and the map is injective because it is injective on functions.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:subgraph}
Let $q=p^a$ with $p$ prime and $a\ge1$, let $m\ge q$, and put $N=m+q-1$ and
$K=K_{m+1,N}$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item The $p$-primary part of $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$ has exactly one cyclic summand of order
      $q$, and all its other cyclic summands have order less than $q$.
\item For every proper subgraph $C$ of $K$, the exponent of $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}/q)$ is less
      than $q$.  Also $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})=0$.  Consequently $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ contains no
      element of order $q$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
(1) By Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} with $r=q$, the $p$-primary part is
$\bigoplus_{i=0}^{q-1}\bigl(\mathbb{Z}/p^{v_p(q-i)}\bigr)^{\binom Ni-\binom N{i-1}}$.  For $i=0$ the
exponent is $a$ and the multiplicity is $1$; for $1\le i\le q-1$ we have
$v_p(q-i)=v_p(i)\le a-1$.

(2) Let $G=H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z}/q)$.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:top}, Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(1) and the
proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors},
\[
G\cong\ker(U_{q-1}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(\operatorname{coker} U_{q-1},\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\mathbb{Z}/q\oplus H,
\]
where, since $\operatorname{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/d,\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(d,q)$, the group $H$ is a direct sum of cyclic
groups of order $p^{v_p(i)}$ with $1\le i\le q-1$; hence $p^{a-1}H=0$.

The constant function $\mathbf 1$ lies in $G$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(2)) and has order
$q$, since it is a vector with entries $1$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/q)^{\binom{[N]}{q-1}}$.  Write
$\mathbf 1=(u,h)$ in $\mathbb{Z}/q\oplus H$; then $p^{a-1}\mathbf 1=(p^{a-1}u,0)\ne0$, so $u$ is a
unit modulo $p$.  Now let $x=(u',h')\in G$ have order $q$.  Again $u'$ is a unit, and
$y:=x-u'u^{-1}\mathbf 1\in H$ satisfies $p^{a-1}y=0$.  Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orderq}
x=c\,\mathbf 1+y,\qquad c\in(\mathbb{Z}/q)^\times,\quad p^{a-1}y=0 .
\end{equation}
In terms of matching functions, $\mathbf 1$ is $F_0(M)=(-1)^{p(\alpha(M))}$, and $y(M)$
lies in $p\mathbb{Z}/q$ for every $m$-matching $M$, because $p^{a-1}y(M)=0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/q$.  Hence
$x(M)\equiv\pm c\not\equiv0\pmod p$: \emph{every element of order $q$ in $G$ is nonzero
on every $m$-matching of $K$.}

Let $C\subsetneq K$ and let $e$ be an edge of $K$ not in $C$.  The edge $e$ lies in
some $m$-matching $M$ of $K$: match its $A$-endpoint to its $B$-endpoint and $m-1$ of
the remaining $m$ vertices of $A$ into the remaining $m+q-2\ge m-1$ vertices of $B$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:extend}, $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}/q)$ embeds in $G$, and every element in its
image vanishes on $M$.  So the image contains no element of order $q$, and
$H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}/q)$ has exponent less than $q$.

Finally, $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ embeds in $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:extend}, so the
universal coefficient theorem gives $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}),\mathbb{Z}/q)$.
Since $\operatorname{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/p^j,\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p^{\min(j,a)}$, the exponent of this group is less than
$q$ exactly when $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ has no $p$-primary cyclic summand of order $\ge q$,
i.e.\ no element of order $q$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{cor:subgraphmin}
For every prime power $q$ and every $m\ge q$, the graph $K_{m+1,m+q-1}$ is minimal among
its subgraphs with respect to elements of order $q$ in $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m)$: it has exactly
one $p$-primary cyclic summand of order $q$, and no proper subgraph has an element of
order $q$.
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:primepower}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item For $a=1$ the group $H$ in the proof is zero, so $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{F}_p)\cong\mathbb{F}_p$.  This
      reproves Lemma~\ref{lem:kerU}(3) from Wilson's diagonal form instead of his rank
      formula.
\item The restriction to prime powers is necessary.  For $q=6$, the proper subgraph
      $K_{m+1,m+4}$ of $K_{m+1,m+5}$ already has cyclic summands $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}/3$ in
      $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} with $r=5$), hence elements of order
      $6$ and a direct summand $\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$; see
      Corollaries~\ref{cor:orderk} and~\ref{cor:orderk-minimal}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:kunneth}
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $\Gamma=\Gamma_1\sqcup\Gamma_2$.  Then $H_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ has
$p$-torsion if and only if some $H_2(\mathbb{B}_a\Gamma_i)$ with $a\le n$ has $p$-torsion and
$\operatorname{UConf}_{n-a}(\Gamma_{3-i})\ne\varnothing$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Apply the K\"unneth formula to
$\operatorname{UConf}_n\Gamma=\bigsqcup_{a+b=n}\operatorname{UConf}_a\Gamma_1\times\operatorname{UConf}_b\Gamma_2$.  The terms
$\operatorname{Tor}(H_0,H_1)$ vanish because $H_0$ is free, and $H_1\otimes H_1$ has no odd torsion by
Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:shape}
Let $\Gamma\preceq K$.  Then $\Gamma$ is homeomorphic to a disjoint union
$(\Lambda\cup P)\sqcup J$, where:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item $\Lambda$ is a subgraph of $K$, obtained by deleting vertices and edges;
\item $P$ is a set of pendant edges attached at vertices of $\Lambda$;
\item $J$ is a disjoint union of arcs and points.
\end{itemize}
If $\Gamma\prec K$, then $\Lambda\ne K$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Let $\Gamma$ be a subgraph of a subdivision $K'$ of $K$.  Each edge $f=xy$ of $K$
becomes a path $\pi_f$ in $K'$, and $\Gamma\cap\pi_f$ is one of the following:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item all of $\pi_f$ (put $f$ into $\Lambda$);
\item a union of subpaths, where a subpath containing $x$ or $y$ is a pendant edge at
      that vertex, and every other subpath is an arc or a point in $J$.
\end{itemize}
The vertices of $K$ lying in $\Gamma$ are the vertices of $\Lambda$.  If $\Lambda=K$, then every
path $\pi_f$ is fully contained in $\Gamma$, so $P=J=\varnothing$ and $\Gamma\cong K$.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:closed}
Let $K$ be a graph and $\Gamma$ a connected graph.  Then $\Gamma\preceq K$ if and only if
$\Gamma$ is homeomorphic to a closed connected subspace of $K$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
A subgraph of a subdivision of $K$ is a closed subspace of the
underlying space of $K$, so the forward implication is immediate.
Conversely, let $A\subseteq K$ be a closed subspace homeomorphic to
$\Gamma$. Since $\Gamma$ is a connected finite graph, $A$ is compact
and path-connected.

After subdividing every loop edge of $K$, we may assume that each
closed edge is an embedded interval. If $A$ is a point, the conclusion
follows by making that point a vertex if necessary. If $A$ is contained
in a closed edge, compactness and connectedness imply that it is a
closed interval or a point, and subdivision at its endpoints gives the
conclusion.

Suppose now that $A$ is not contained in any closed edge. Let $e$ be a
closed edge and let $x\in A\cap e^\circ$. Choose $y\in A\setminus e$
and a path in $A$ from $x$ to $y$. At the first time this path exits
$e^\circ$, it reaches an endpoint of $e$. The part of the path before
and including that exit is a connected subset of $e$ containing $x$
and that endpoint, so it contains the whole interval between them.
Thus every point of $A\cap e^\circ$ is joined within $A\cap e$ to an
endpoint of $e$.

It follows that $A\cap e$ is empty or is a union of at most two closed
intervals, each containing an endpoint of $e$; intervals consisting of
a single endpoint are allowed. There are only finitely many edges.
Subdivide $K$ at the endpoints of these intervals that lie in edge
interiors. Then $A$ is a connected subgraph of the resulting
subdivision. Since $\Gamma$ is homeomorphic to $A$, this proves
$\Gamma\preceq K$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:topminimal}
Let $q=p^a$ with $p$ prime and $a\ge1$, let $m\ge q$, and put $K=K_{m+1,m+q-1}$.  If
$\Gamma\prec K$, then $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ has no element of order $q$.  Thus $K$ is
minimal in the topological minor order for elements of order $q$ in this degree and
particle number.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:shape}, write $\Gamma\cong(\Lambda\cup P)\sqcup J$, where $\Lambda\subsetneq K$,
$P$ consists of pendant edges and $J$ consists of arcs and points.
Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone}, including its isolated-vertex case, removes all edges
of $P$ without changing the torsion in the indicated bidegree.  The same corollary
removes $J$.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reduce}
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})\cong\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Lambda;\mathbb{Z}).
\end{equation}
The latter group has no element of order $q$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:subgraph}.  The full
graph $K$ has such an element by Theorem~\ref{thm:explicitgen}.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:minimal}
$H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5})$ contains $\mathbb{Z}/3$, and $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Gamma)$ has no odd torsion for every
$\Gamma\prec K_{4,5}$.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
The first assertion is Corollary~\ref{cor:exact}.  For a proper topological minor use
\eqref{eq:reduce} with $m=q=3$ to reduce to a proper subgraph $\Lambda\subsetneq K_{4,5}$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:subgraph} excludes $3$-torsion.  For an odd prime $p\ge5$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:extend} embeds $H_3(\mathbb{B}_3\Lambda;\mathbb{F}_p)$ into
$H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5};\mathbb{F}_p)\cong T_{\mathbb{F}_p}(5)=0$.  Also $H_3(\mathbb{B}_3\Lambda;\mathbb{Z})=0$ by integral extension
by zero.  The universal coefficient theorem therefore excludes $p$-torsion in
$H_2(\mathbb{B}_3\Lambda;\mathbb{Z})$ for all such $p$.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:threelevels}
For $q=3$ the class $[z_3]\in H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,5})$ of order $3$ is minimal in three
independent senses.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Homological degree.}  For every finite graph $\Gamma$ and every $n$, the
      groups $H_0(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ and $H_1(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ have no $3$-torsion: $H_0$ is free,
      and $H_1$ has only $2$-torsion by Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}.  Thus $3$-torsion first
      occurs in degree $2$, for any graph whatsoever.
\item \emph{Particle number.}  In degree $2$, torsion of any kind requires at least
      three particles (Observation~\ref{obs:top}).
\item \emph{The graph.}  With three particles and in degree $2$, no $\Gamma\prec K_{4,5}$
      has $3$-torsion (Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal}), while $K_{4,5}$ does.
\end{enumerate}
For a general prime power $q$, levels (2) and (3) hold with
\[
(2,3,K_{4,5})\quad\text{replaced by}\quad(q-1,q,K_{q+1,2q-1}),
\]
by Observation~\ref{obs:top} and Theorem~\ref{thm:topminimal};
level (1), namely that an element of order $q$ never occurs in $H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ with
$i<q-1$, is known only for $q=2,3$ (Question~\ref{q:kuratowski}(2)). 
For $m>q$, the examples in degree $m-1$ do not attain the smallest
homological degree in which this paper constructs an element of order
$q$: the graph $K_{q+1,2q-1}$ already provides such an example in degree
$q-1$. This is a comparison between examples on different graphs; it
does not assert that the corresponding torsion class survives under
inclusion into a larger graph.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:contract}
Let $K_{a,b}$ have bipartition $A\sqcup B$, let $F$ be a set of edges, and let
$M=K_{a,b}/F$.  Let
\[
C_1,\ldots,C_t
\]
be the nontrivial branch sets, and write
\[
\alpha_i=|C_i\cap A|,\qquad \beta_i=|C_i\cap B|.
\]
Thus $\alpha_i,\beta_i\ge1$.  Put
\[
s=a-\sum_{i=1}^t\alpha_i,\qquad
s'=b-\sum_{i=1}^t\beta_i.
\]
After deleting loops and retaining one edge in each parallel class, the resulting
simple graph is
\[
L\cong K_t+K_{s,s'}.
\]
In particular
\[
t+s=a-\sum_{i=1}^t(\alpha_i-1),\qquad
t+s'=b-\sum_{i=1}^t(\beta_i-1).
\]

More precisely, if $i\ne j$, the number of edges of $M$ joining the vertices
corresponding to $C_i$ and $C_j$ is
\[
\alpha_i\beta_j+\beta_i\alpha_j.
\]
The multiplicity between $C_i$ and a singleton vertex originating in $A$ is
$\beta_i$, and that between $C_i$ and a singleton originating in $B$ is $\alpha_i$.
If $F_i=F\cap E(K_{a,b}[C_i])$, then the number of loops at the vertex corresponding
to $C_i$ is
\[
\alpha_i\beta_i-|F_i|.
\]
In particular, the existence of a loop at $C_i$ forces
$\alpha_i,\beta_i\ge2$.

Conversely, every triple
\[
t\ge1,\qquad 0\le s\le a-t,\qquad 0\le s'\le b-t
\]
occurs as the simple reduction of a contraction of $K_{a,b}$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
The vertices of $M$ are the vertex sets of the connected components of $(V,F)$.
Every nontrivial component meets both $A$ and $B$, while every other branch set is a
singleton.  Distinct branch sets are joined by all original edges running from the
$A$-part of one to the $B$-part of the other.  This gives the stated multiplicities
and shows that, after simplification, every mixed branch set is universal, the
remaining $A$-singletons and $B$-singletons span $K_{s,s'}$, and hence
$L\cong K_t+K_{s,s'}$.

Inside $C_i$ there are $\alpha_i\beta_i$ original edges, of which precisely the
edges of $F_i$ are contracted; all the others become loops.  Since $F_i$ connects
$C_i$, one has $|F_i|\ge\alpha_i+\beta_i-1$, so a loop can occur only when
$(\alpha_i-1)(\beta_i-1)>0$.

For the converse, choose disjoint subsets
\[
A=A_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_t\sqcup A_0,\qquad
B=B_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup B_t\sqcup B_0
\]
with every $A_i,B_i$ nonempty, $|A_0|=s$ and $|B_0|=s'$.  In each complete bipartite
graph $K_{A_i,B_i}$ choose a spanning tree and let $F$ be the union of these $t$
trees.  Its nontrivial branch sets are exactly $A_i\sqcup B_i$, so the simple
reduction is $K_t+K_{s,s'}$.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:join-top}
Let
\[
J=K_t+K_{s,b},\qquad d=t+s,
\]
and let $n\ge1$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item If $d\le n$, then
\[
H_n(\mathbb{B}_nJ;R)=0
\]
for every commutative ring $R$.
\item If $n\ge2$ and $d=n+1$, let $D$ be the union of the $K_t$-vertices and the
$s$-part of $K_{s,b}$.  Then restriction to the spanning complete bipartite graph
$K_{D,B}\cong K_{n+1,b}$ induces
\[
H_n(\mathbb{B}_nJ;R)\cong H_n(\mathbb{B}_nK_{n+1,b};R)
\]
for every commutative ring $R$.
The right-hand side is zero for $b\le n$; if $b=n+\rho-1$ with $\rho\ge2$,
it is $\ker(U_{\rho-1}(n+\rho-1)\otimes R)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:top}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Every edge of $J$ has at least one endpoint in $D$.

If $d<n$, there is no $n$-matching.  Suppose $d=n$.  Every $n$-matching uses every
vertex of $D$ and contains no edge with both endpoints in $D$.  Remove one edge
$db$ from such a matching.  In the relation \eqref{eq:Z} at the free vertex $b$,
all vertices of $D$ except $d$ are occupied, so the relation has the single term
$F(db,M')$.  Hence every top cycle vanishes.

Now assume $d=n+1$ and $n\ge2$.  If an $n$-matching $M$ contains an edge with both
endpoints in $D$, it contains exactly one such edge and the remaining $n-1$ edges
join $D$ to $B$.  Removing one of those $D$--$B$ edges and applying
\eqref{eq:Z} at its $B$-endpoint again gives a single-term relation, so every top
cycle vanishes on $M$.  Thus every top cycle is supported on the matchings of the
spanning $K_{D,B}$.  Conversely, extension by zero from $K_{D,B}$ to $J$ gives a
top cycle by Lemma~\ref{lem:extend}.  Restriction and extension by zero are inverse.
If $b<n$, the bipartite graph has no $n$-matching.  If $b=n$, removing an edge
from an $n$-matching leaves only one free $B$-vertex, so the relation
\eqref{eq:Z} at its $D$-endpoint has a single term and forces the matching value
to vanish.  For $b=n+\rho-1$ with $\rho\ge2$, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:top}.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:inherit}
Let $\Gamma$ be a simple graph, $m\ge1$ and $q=p^a$ a prime power.  Suppose
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\exp H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z}/q)<q.
\]
Then $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ has no element of order $q$ for every subgraph
$C\subseteq\Gamma$.  For $q=p$ prime, the second hypothesis is simply
$H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{F}_p)=0$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:extend} embeds both $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ and
$H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}/q)$ into the corresponding groups for $\Gamma$.  Hence the integral top
group of $C$ is zero and the exponent of its $\mathbb{Z}/q$ top homology is less than $q$.
The universal coefficient theorem gives
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z}),\mathbb{Z}/q).
\]
An element of order $q=p^a$ in $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ would contribute a cyclic summand of
order $q$ to the right-hand side, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:minor-threshold}
Let $M=K_{a,b}/F$, and let
\[
K_t+K_{s,s'}
\]
be its simple reduction as in Lemma~\ref{lem:contract}, where $s$ refers to the
singleton vertices originating in the $a$-part.  Fix $n\ge1$.  If
\[
t+s\le n,
\]
then for every $\Gamma\preceq M$,
\[
H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})
\]
is torsion-free.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
The case $n=1$ is immediate because $H_0$ is free abelian.  Assume $n\ge2$.
By the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:shape}, applied to the multigraph $M$, one may write
\[
\Gamma\cong(\Lambda\cup P)\sqcup J,
\]
where $\Lambda\subseteq M$, $P$ is a collection of pendant edges and $J$ is a disjoint
union of arcs and points.  Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone} removes $P$ and $J$
without changing the torsion in $H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n)$, so it is enough to treat $\Lambda$.

We use induction first on $n$ and, for fixed $n$, on the number of loops plus the
number of edges in excess of one in the parallel classes of $\Lambda$.
This family is closed under vertex deletion: deleting vertices of $M$ amounts to
deleting their entire branch sets from $K_{a,b}$ and restricting $F$ to the
remaining vertices.  The result is a contraction of the complete bipartite graph
on the remaining original vertices (allowing an empty part).  Thus the outer
induction applies to the graphs $M-v$ and $M-\{u,w\}$ below.  When it reaches
particle number one, torsion vanishes directly in $H_0$.

If $\Lambda$ is simple, it is a subgraph of $K_t+K_{s,s'}$.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:join-top}(1),
\[
H_n(\mathbb{B}_n(K_t+K_{s,s'});R)=0
\]
for every commutative ring $R$.  Extension by zero therefore gives
$H_n(\mathbb{B}_n\Lambda;R)=0$ for every $R$.  Taking $R=\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ and using the universal
coefficient theorem shows that $H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Lambda;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion-free.

Suppose next that $\Lambda=\Lambda_0\cup e'$ and $e'$ is parallel to an edge $e=uw$ of $\Lambda_0$.
Theorem~\ref{prop:parallel-top} gives
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Lambda)
\cong
\operatorname{Tors} H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Lambda_0)
\oplus
\operatorname{Tors} H_{n-2}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}(\Lambda_0)_{uw}).
\]
The first summand vanishes by the inner induction.  Exploding both $u$ and $w$
turns every edge incident to $u$ or $w$ into a pendant edge or an isolated arc.
After removing those pieces, the remaining core is a subgraph of $M-\{u,w\}$.
A parallel class in a contraction of a complete bipartite graph cannot join an
$A$-singleton to a $B$-singleton; hence at least one of $u,w$ is a mixed branch set.
Deleting $u,w$ therefore lowers $t+s$ by at least one.  The simple reduction of
$M-\{u,w\}$ consequently has parameter at most
\[
(t+s)-1\le n-1.
\]
The outer induction, together with Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone}, shows that the
second summand also vanishes.

Now suppose that $\Lambda$ contains a loop $e_0$ at $v$.  A loop in $M$ can occur only
at a mixed branch set, by Lemma~\ref{lem:contract}.  If $v$ is nonisolated after
deleting $e_0$, Theorem~\ref{cor:loop} in the bidegree $(n-1,n)$ gives
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n\Lambda)
\cong
\operatorname{Tors} H_{n-1}(\mathbb{B}_n(\Lambda-e_0))
\oplus
\operatorname{Tors} H_{n-2}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}(\Lambda-e_0)_v).
\]
The first term vanishes by the inner induction.  After exploding $v$, the remaining
core is a subgraph of $M-v$, whose simple reduction has parameter
$(t+s)-1\le n-1$; the second term therefore vanishes by the outer induction.

Finally, if the loop is an isolated circle component, write $\Lambda=S^1\sqcup \Lambda'$.  Since
$\operatorname{UConf}_k(S^1)\simeq S^1$ for $k\ge1$, its homology is free and concentrated in
degrees $0$ and $1$.  The K\"unneth formula in total degree $n-1$ reduces possible
torsion either to the same group for $\Lambda'$ with $n$ particles, or to
$H_{n-2}(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Lambda')$.  The former vanishes by the inner induction and the latter by
the outer induction, because deleting the mixed branch set supporting the loop lowers
$t+s$ by one.  This completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:strongmin}
Let
\[
q=p^a,\qquad a\ge1,\qquad m\ge q,
\qquad K=K_{m+1,m+q-1}.
\]
If $\Gamma<K$ in the order generated by edge deletion, vertex deletion, edge
contraction and subdivision, up to homeomorphism, then
\[
H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})
\]
has no element of order $q$.  Thus $K_{m+1,m+q-1}$ is minimal for order-$q$ torsion
in the full minor order, with loops and parallel edges retained after contraction.
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
The full graph $K$ has an element of order $q$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:explicitgen}.
Let $\Gamma\preceq K/F$.  If $F=\varnothing$, the assertion is
Theorem~\ref{thm:topminimal}, so assume $F\ne\varnothing$ and put
\[
M=K/F.
\]
Use Lemma~\ref{lem:contract} with the $(m+1)$-vertex part as the first bipartition
class, and write the simple reduction of $M$ as
\[
L=K_t+K_{s,s'}.
\]
Set
\[
d=t+s.
\]
Since
\[
d=m+1-\sum_{i=1}^t(\alpha_i-1),
\]
one has $d\le m+1$.

If $d\le m$, Lemma~\ref{lem:minor-threshold} gives the stronger conclusion that
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion-free.  It remains to consider $d=m+1$.

The equality $d=m+1$ forces
\[
\alpha_1=\cdots=\alpha_t=1.
\]
Hence $M$ has no loops.  Moreover $t\ge1$ and
\[
s'=m+q-1-\sum_{i=1}^t\beta_i\le m+q-2.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:join-top}(2),
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mL;R)\cong H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,s'};R).
\]
If $s'\le m$, the right side is zero for every $R$.  If $s'>m$, put
$r=s'-m+1$.  Then
\[
2\le r\le q-1\le m.
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors} therefore gives $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mL;\mathbb{Z})=0$, and, with coefficients
in $\mathbb{Z}/q$, $H_m(\mathbb{B}_mL;\mathbb{Z}/q)$ is a direct sum of groups $(\mathbb{Z}/q)[j]\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(j,q)$ with
$2\le j\le r<q$, hence has exponent less than $q$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:inherit},
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mC;\mathbb{Z})$ has no element of order $q$ for every simple subgraph $C\subseteq L$.

Now let $\Lambda\subseteq M$ be an arbitrary subgraph, and let $C$ be obtained from $\Lambda$
by retaining one edge in each parallel class.  There are no loops.  We add the
remaining parallel edges back one at a time.  Because every mixed branch set has
$\alpha_i=1$, a parallel class of $M$ is either between two mixed branch sets or
between a mixed branch set and an $A$-singleton; a mixed branch set and a
$B$-singleton are joined by only one edge.  Hence the two endpoints $u,w$ of every
extra parallel edge both contribute to $d=t+s$.  Deleting them lowers $d$ by two.

Suppose $\Lambda_1=\Lambda_0\cup e'$ is one step in this reconstruction.  By
Theorem~\ref{prop:parallel-top},
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Lambda_1)
\cong
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Lambda_0)
\oplus
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-2}(\mathbb{B}_{m-1}(\Lambda_0)_{uw}).
\]
After exploding $u,w$ and removing the resulting pendant edges and isolated arcs,
the remaining core is a subgraph of $M-\{u,w\}$.  Its simple reduction has parameter
\[
d-2=m-1.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:minor-threshold}, now with $n=m-1$, shows that the second summand is
torsion-free.  Thus adding contraction-created parallel edges does not change the
torsion subgroup in the bidegree $(m-1,m)$.  It follows that $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Lambda)$ has no
element of order $q$.

Finally, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:shape} applies to the multigraph $M$, so
\[
\Gamma\cong(\Lambda\cup P)\sqcup J
\]
with $P$ a collection of pendant edges and $J$ a disjoint union of arcs and points.
Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone} removes $P$ and $J$ without changing the torsion in
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m)$.  The result follows.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- corollary-17: body_md -->
\label{cor:orderk-minimal}
Let $k\ge2$, let $q=q(k)$ be the largest prime power dividing $k$, and let $m\ge q$.
Then $K=K_{m+1,m+q-1}$ is minimal in the full minor order for elements of order $k$
in $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m)$: the group $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK;\mathbb{Z})$ has a direct summand $\mathbb{Z}/k$,
whereas $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ has no element of order $k$ for every $\Gamma<K$.
<!-- end corollary-17 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{cor:orderk} gives the direct summand $\mathbb{Z}/k$ for $K$.
If $x\in H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ had order $k$ for a proper minor $\Gamma<K$,
then $(k/q)x$ would have order $q$, contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:strongmin}.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- corollary-18: body_md -->
\label{cor:fullminor-k45}
$K_{4,5}$ is minimal in the full minor order for odd torsion in $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3)$.
<!-- end corollary-18 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
The full graph has $3$-torsion by Corollary~\ref{cor:exact}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:strongmin} with $(q,m)=(3,3)$ excludes $3$-torsion from every
proper minor.  It remains to exclude torsion at odd primes $p\ge5$.

Write $\Gamma\preceq M=K_{4,5}/F$.  If $F=\varnothing$, this follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal}.  If $F\ne\varnothing$, use the notation $d=t+s$ of
the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:strongmin}.  For $d\le3$, Lemma~\ref{lem:minor-threshold}
excludes all torsion.  For $d=4$, the simple reduction $L$ satisfies
$H_3(\mathbb{B}_3L;R)\cong H_3(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,s'};R)$ with $s'\le4$.  This group is zero for
$s'\le3$ and is $R[2]$ for $s'=4$.  In particular it vanishes for $R=\mathbb{Z}$ and
$R=\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p$ odd.  Extension by zero and the universal coefficient theorem
therefore exclude odd torsion for every simple subgraph of $L$.  As proved in
Theorem~\ref{thm:strongmin}, restoring the parallel edges in the case $d=m+1$
does not change the torsion subgroup.  Finally Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone}
removes the pendant edges and isolated arcs and points arising from subdivisions.
This excludes every odd prime and proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:strongmin} establishes prime-power minimality in the full
      multigraph minor order.  The key additional input beyond the simple-core
      argument is Theorem~\ref{prop:parallel-top}: in bidegree $(m-1,m)$ the
      torsion splits as a direct sum, so no nontrivial extension can create an
      element of order $q$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:minor-threshold} makes the additional
      summands vanish for the contraction-created parallel edges when $d=m+1$,
      and handles all loops and parallel edges when $d\le m$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:topminor}
In the usual definition, $\Gamma$ is a topological minor of $K$ if some subdivision of
$\Gamma$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $K$.  Our order $\preceq$ contains this order,
and it is strictly larger. 
Deleting an open subinterval whose closure is contained in the interior
of an edge $xy$ of $K$ leaves pendant stubs at both $x$ and $y$, and the
two stubs cannot in general be realized by two distinct edges of $K$.
For instance, $(K_{4,5}\setminus a_1b_1)$ with pendant edges at
$a_1$ and at $b_1$ has $11$ vertices, so no subdivision of it is a subgraph of
$K_{4,5}$, yet it is $\prec K_{4,5}$.  Minimality with respect to $\preceq$, as in
Theorems~\ref{thm:topminimal} and~\ref{thm:minimal}, is therefore the stronger
statement.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:closed}, for connected $\Gamma$ the relation
$\Gamma\preceq K$ means exactly that $\Gamma$ is homeomorphic to a closed connected
subspace of $K$; in general it means that $\Gamma$ is homeomorphic to a closed subspace
of $K$ with finitely many components.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:twotorsion}
For $2$-torsion, $K_{4,5}$ is not minimal. Corollary~\ref{cor:r2} gives
\[
\operatorname{Tors} H_2(\mathbb{B}_3K_{4,4})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2,
\]
and $K_{4,4}$ is minimal
for $2$-torsion in $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:topminimal} with $(q,m)=(2,3)$.  It is
not the only minimal graph: see Section~\ref{sec:complete}.
Theorem~\ref{thm:topminimal} establishes prime-power minimality in the topological minor
order for every $m\ge q$, not just for $(q,m)=(2,2)$ or $(3,3)$.  The extra input is the
exact pendant splitting: in degree $m-1$ with $m$ particles its new terms are free for
dimensional reasons, irrespective of torsion in lower degrees at larger particle
numbers.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:complete}
Let $m\ge2$.  For every commutative ring $R$,
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{2m+1};R)\cong R[2],
\]
spanned by the class of the constant matching function when $2R=0$.
Consequently,
\[
H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{2m+1};\mathbb{Z})=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{2m+1};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2 .
\]
Moreover, if $\Gamma\prec K_{2m+1}$, then $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Gamma;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion-free.  In
particular $K_{2m+1}$ is minimal in the order $\preceq$ for $2$-torsion in
$H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m)$, and $K_{m+1,m+1}$ and $K_{2m+1}$ are incomparable in this order.
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Let $F$ be a matching function on $K_{2m+1}$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:Zcycles}.  An
$(m-1)$-matching $M'$ leaves exactly three free vertices, which are pairwise adjacent.
Hence every relation \eqref{eq:Z} has exactly two terms, and the three relations at the
free vertices of $M'$ are those of Example~\ref{ex:C3}: for free vertices $x,y,f$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rotation}
F(xy,M')=F(yf,M')=F(fx,M').
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 1: $2F=0$.}  Let $M$ be an $m$-matching, and split $M=N\cup M''$ with $N$
consisting of two edges of $M$; this uses $m\ge2$.  Let $S$ be the set of five vertices
not covered by $M''$, and define $G(N')=F(N',M'')$ for every ordered oriented
$2$-matching $N'$ of the complete graph $K_5$ on $S$, with the edges of $N'$ listed
first.  For a $1$-matching $N''$ of $K_5[S]$ and a vertex $v\in S$ not covered by it,
the free neighbours of $v$ in $K_{2m+1}$ relative to $N''\cup M''$ are exactly the two
remaining vertices of $S$.  So the relations \eqref{eq:Z} of $K_{2m+1}$ at
$(N''\cup M'',v)$ are precisely the relations of $K_5$ at $(N'',v)$, and $G$ is a matching
function of $K_5$ with two particles.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:KP} in the form of
\cite[Theorem~3.16]{KP}, $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_5)\cong\mathbb{Z}^6\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, and Gal's formula gives
$\chi(\mathbb{B}_2K_5)=-5$, so $H_2(\mathbb{B}_2K_5;\mathbb{Z})=0$.  The universal coefficient theorem yields
$H_2(\mathbb{B}_2K_5;R)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/2,R)=R[2]$, so $2G=0$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:Zcycles}.  In particular $2F(M)=0$.

\emph{Step 2: connectivity.}  Call two $m$-matchings adjacent if one is obtained from
the other by replacing an edge $xy$ by $yf$ or $fx$, where $f$ is the vertex missed by
the first; by \eqref{eq:rotation} and Step~1, $F$ takes the same value on adjacent
matchings, whatever their orientation and order.  We claim that this graph on
$m$-matchings is connected.  Replacing $xy\in M$ by $fx$ moves the missed vertex from
$f$ to $y$, so every vertex can be made the missed one.  Given $M$ missing $f$ and two
edges $xy,zw\in M$, the three replacements $xy\to fx$, $zw\to yz$, $fx\to xw$ produce
the matching $M\setminus\{xy,zw\}\cup\{xw,yz\}$, again missing $f$.  Such exchanges
generate all perfect matchings of $K_{2m+1}\setminus f$, which proves the claim.

\emph{Step 3: the module.}  By Steps~1 and~2, $F$ is determined by the single value
$c=F(M_0)\in R[2]$ of a fixed matching $M_0$, and $F$ takes the value $c$ on every ordered
oriented $m$-matching.  Conversely, for $c\in R[2]$ the function with constant value $c$
is alternating and odd under reversal, because $c=-c$, and satisfies every relation
\eqref{eq:Z}, because each relation has two terms and $c+c=0$.  Hence
$H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{2m+1};R)\cong R[2]$.

\emph{Step 4: torsion.}  With $R=\mathbb{Z}$ the top homology vanishes, so the universal
coefficient theorem gives $H_m(\,\cdot\,;\mathbb{Z}/q)\cong\operatorname{Tor}(H_{m-1},\mathbb{Z}/q)$.  For $q=2$ this
is $\mathbb{F}_2$, for $q=4$ it is $\mathbb{Z}/2$, and for odd primes it is $0$; as in the proof of
Corollary~\ref{cor:r2}, $\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{2m+1})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$.

\emph{Step 5: minimality.} Let $\Gamma\prec K_{2m+1}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:shape},
$\Gamma\cong(\Lambda\cup P)\sqcup J$ with $\Lambda\subsetneq K_{2m+1}$.
Theorem~\ref{cor:topminusone} removes the pendant edges $P$ and the
disjoint arcs and points $J$ without changing the full torsion subgroup
in degree $m-1$ and weight $m$. It therefore suffices to treat $\Lambda$.
Choose an edge $e$ of $K_{2m+1}$ missing from $\Lambda$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:extend}, every top matching function on $\Lambda$ extends by zero
to one on $K_{2m+1}$. By Steps~1--3 this extension is constant on all
$m$-matchings. There exists an $m$-matching containing $e$: pair any
$2m-2$ of the $2m-1$ remaining vertices. Its value under the extension
is zero, so the constant is zero. Thus $H_m(\mathbb{B}_m\Lambda;R)=0$ for every $R$.
The universal coefficient theorem, with $R=\mathbb{F}_\ell$ for each prime $\ell$,
now shows that $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_m\Lambda;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion-free.
Finally, $K_{m+1,m+1}$ has $2m+2$ vertices of degree at least three,
whereas $K_{2m+1}$ has only $2m+1$; and $K_{2m+1}$ has vertices of degree
$2m>m+1$, the maximum degree in $K_{m+1,m+1}$. These obstructions persist
under subdivision and passage to a subgraph, so the two graphs are
incomparable in the order $\preceq$.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item As in Section~\ref{sec:explicit}, the class of the constant function is
      represented by a chain $w$ which is a sum of the cubes of all $m$-matchings of
      $K_{2m+1}$ with coefficients $\pm1$.  Since $\bar w$ is a mod-$2$ cycle,
      $\partial w=2z$ for an integral $(m-1)$-chain $z$, which is a cycle, and
      $[z]=\beta[\bar w]$ generates $\operatorname{Tors} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{2m+1})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ because the
      Bockstein is injective.  This is the analogue of Theorem~B for $q=2$.
\item For $m=1$ the statement fails: $K_3$ is a circle and $H_1(\mathbb{B}_1K_3;R)\cong R$.  The
      argument breaks down in Step~1, which needs two edges in a matching.
\item Thus, for three particles, $2$-torsion in $H_2$ has at least the two incomparable
      minimal graphs $K_{4,4}$ and $K_7$.  Unlike odd torsion, it can also be created by
      attaching a lollipop: by Theorem~\ref{cor:loop}, $\operatorname{Tors}_2H_2(\mathbb{B}_3)$ of
      $\Delta\cup(\text{lollipop at }x)$ contains $\operatorname{Tors}_2H_1(\mathbb{B}_2(\Delta\cup\text{pendant at }x))$,
      which is $\mathbb{Z}/2$ for $\Delta=K_{3,3}$ or $K_5$ (Example~\ref{ex:loopfail}).  These
      graphs are again incomparable with $K_{4,4}$ and $K_7$.  A complete list of the
      minimal graphs with $2$-torsion in $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3)$ is not known to us.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{q:betti}
Let $m\ge4$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item Determine the Betti numbers of $\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1}$. The torsion
      in degree $m-1$ is known for every $r\ge0$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:exacttors}), and
      for $1\le r\le m-1$ the theta subgroup contributes free rank
      $\binom{m+r-1}{r}-\binom{m+r-1}{r-1}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:theta-injective},
      but the remaining free classes are not determined by that presentation.
\item Is $\operatorname{rank}_\mathbb{Z} H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{m+1,m+r-1};\mathbb{Z})$ given by a polynomial in $r$ for
      every $r\ge m$? More generally, for fixed $m$ and $i<m$, are the free rank and
      the prime-power torsion multiplicities of $H_i(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})$ eventually
      polynomial in $a$ and $b$, and with what ranges of validity?
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{q:small-prime-vanishing}
Let $m\ge4$ and $a,b\ge2m-1$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item For an odd prime $p<m$, does
      $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{F}_p)-\operatorname{rank} H_m(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})$ vanish? If not,
      describe its values in terms of the modular slot representations
      $D_m(a;\mathbb{F}_p)$ and $D_m(b;\mathbb{F}_p)$. The first case not covered by
      Theorem~\ref{rep:thm:generalvanishing} is $m=4$, $p=3$.
\item Determine the cyclic factors of the $2$-primary subgroup of
      $H_{m-1}(\mathbb{B}_mK_{a,b};\mathbb{Z})$ from the integral slot modules. What is the
      optimal exponent bound for fixed $m$, and when do factors of order $4$ or
      higher occur? The first case is $m=4$, $a,b\ge7$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{q:first-vanishing}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $q=p^a$ with $a\ge1$, and let $\tau_q$ be the order-$q$
class of Theorem~\ref{thm:explicitgen} on $K_{q+1,2q-1}$. Does its image in
$H_{q-1}(\mathbb{B}_qK_{s,2q-1};\mathbb{Z})$ vanish for some $s\ge q+1$? If so, determine the
least such $s$. At which values of $s$, if any, does the entire $p$-primary
torsion vanish? For $a=1$, Corollary~\ref{rep:cor:allprimecounterexample} gives
vanishing at $s=2p-1$; is this the first value,
and in particular does $\tau_5$ survive in $H_4(\mathbb{B}_5K_{7,9};\mathbb{Z})$? For $a\ge2$,
even the case $s=2q-1$ is open.
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
\label{q:tableau-cycles}
Can the summands in \eqref{rep:eq:main} be realized by explicit matching
cycles indexed by pairs of standard Young tableaux? Determine the
integral lattice generated by such cycles, its index in the full top
homology, and the maps induced by inclusions of complete bipartite
graphs. Can this construction describe the failure of integral lifting
of modular top cycles, and hence the torsion one degree below?
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- question-5: body_md -->
\label{q:kuratowski}
Let $q=p^a$ be a prime power.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item For $p$ odd, does $p$-torsion in $H_*(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ imply that $\Gamma$ has a
      $K_{p+1,2p-1}$ minor? The restriction to odd primes is essential, since $K_5$
      has $2$-torsion in $H_1(\mathbb{B}_2K_5)$ but no $K_{3,3}$ minor. Already for $p=3$
      and $H_2(\mathbb{B}_3)$ the question is open.
\item Can an element of order $q$ occur in $H_i(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)$ for some finite graph
      $\Gamma$, some $n$, and some $i<q-1$? For $q=2,3$ the answer is no ($H_0$ is
      free, and $H_1$ has only $2$-torsion by Theorem~\ref{thm:KP}); the first open
      cases are $q=4$ in degree $2$ and $q=5$ in degrees $2,3$.
\end{enumerate}
A negative answer to \textup{(2)} would make $K_{q+1,2q-1}$ minimal for order-$q$
torsion in homological degree, particle number, and the order $\preceq$
simultaneously (Remark~\ref{rem:threelevels}).
<!-- end question-5 -->
<!-- question-6: body_md -->
\label{q:parallel}
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite graph with an edge $e=uw$, $u\ne w$, and let
$\Gamma^+$ be obtained by adding an edge parallel to $e$. For every odd prime
$p$ and every $n\ge4$, does the inclusion induce an isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tors}_pH_2(\mathbb{B}_n\Gamma^+)?
\]
Equivalently, with $\Gamma_u$ and $\Gamma_w$ denoting the vertex explosions,
is the group
\[
\operatorname{coker}\!\left(
H_2(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_u)\oplus H_2(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma_w)
\longrightarrow H_2(\mathbb{B}_{n-1}\Gamma)
\right)
\]
free of odd torsion for every $n\ge4$?
<!-- end question-6 -->
